upanishads-katha-1-2-19.plain: Yama, the god of death, teaches the boy Nachiketas that the true Self can never kill or be killed. A person who thinks they are the killer, or the one killed, does not understand what they really are.

upanishads-katha-1-2-20.plain: The Self, your deepest being, is tinier than the tiniest thing and bigger than the biggest, and it lives hidden in the heart. A person who has let go of craving and sorrow can see its greatness, as a gift from the Creator.

upanishads-katha-1-2-21.plain: The Self sits still yet travels far, and lies down yet goes everywhere. Yama asks who but someone like himself can truly know this God, who is both joyful and beyond joy.

upanishads-katha-1-2-22.plain: A wise person knows the Self has no body, even though it lives inside bodies. It never changes while everything around it changes, and it is everywhere. Knowing this, that person never grieves.

upanishads-katha-1-2-23.plain: You cannot reach the Self just by studying the Vedas (holy texts), by being clever, or by learning a lot. The Self reveals itself to the person it chooses and makes that person its own.

upanishads-katha-1-2-24.plain: A person who has not first stopped doing wrong, who is not calm and self-controlled, and whose mind is restless, cannot reach the Self, even with knowledge.

upanishads-katha-1-2-25.plain: Yama asks who can really know where this Great One is. To him, even priests and warriors are like food, and death itself is just a spice added to the meal.

upanishads-katha-1-3-1.plain: Two selves live in the cave of the heart: the individual self, who tastes the results of its own actions, and the highest Self. Those who know Brahman (the ultimate reality), and people who do the special Nachiketa fire ritual three times, call them shadow and light.

upanishads-katha-1-3-2.plain: This is a prayer: may we master the Nachiketa fire ritual, a bridge for those who make offerings, and also come to know the highest, never-ending Brahman, which carries seekers to the shore where there is no fear.

upanishads-katha-1-3-3.plain: Think of yourself like a chariot ride: your true Self is the passenger, your body is the chariot, your thinking mind (buddhi, the power to decide) is the driver, and your everyday mind is the reins.

upanishads-katha-1-3-4.plain: In this picture, your senses are the horses, and the things they want are the roads they run on. When the Self is joined with body, senses and mind, the wise call it the one who experiences and enjoys.

upanishads-katha-1-3-5.plain: If a person lacks good judgment and never holds their mind firmly, their senses run wild, like unruly horses that the driver cannot control.

upanishads-katha-1-3-6.plain: But if a person has good judgment and always holds their mind steady, their senses obey, like well-trained horses obey a good driver.

upanishads-katha-1-3-7.plain: A person without good judgment, who is careless and impure, never reaches the goal. Instead they keep being born again and again.

upanishads-katha-1-3-8.plain: But a person with good judgment, who is careful and pure, reaches the goal, and from there they are never born again.

upanishads-katha-1-3-9.plain: A person who lets wisdom drive and keeps a firm hold on the mind reaches the end of the journey, the highest home of Vishnu (God).

upanishads-katha-1-3-10.plain: There is a ladder of what is deeper: beyond the senses are the things they sense, beyond those is the mind, beyond the mind is the intellect, and beyond the intellect is the Great Self.

upanishads-katha-1-3-11.plain: Beyond the Great Self is the Unmanifest (the hidden source of the world), and beyond that is the Purusha, the Supreme Person. Nothing is beyond the Purusha; it is the final goal.

upanishads-katha-1-3-12.plain: The Self is hidden in every living being and does not show itself openly. But people with a sharp, refined mind can see it.

upanishads-katha-1-3-13.plain: A wise person should quiet their speech into the mind, the mind into the intellect, the intellect into the Great Self, and that into the Self which is perfect peace.

upanishads-chandogya-8-13-1.plain: The seeker declares: I move from the hidden Brahman (the ultimate reality) within my heart to the bright world of Brahman. I shake off all wrongdoing like a horse shaking its hair, and like the moon coming free after an eclipse (Rahu is the demon said to swallow the moon). Leaving the body behind, I reach the world of Brahman that was never made, fulfilled and at peace.

upanishads-chandogya-8-14-1.plain: Space (akasha) is what lets all names and shapes appear. What holds all those names and shapes is Brahman, the deathless Self. The speaker prays to reach the home of Prajapati, the creator god, and to be honored among priests, rulers and all people. He asks never to be reborn into the womb, which he calls the toothless place that still devours.

upanishads-chandogya-8-15-1.plain: This teaching was handed down from the god Brahma to Prajapati, then to Manu, the first man, and then to all people. A person who learns the Vedas (sacred texts) from a teacher while serving him, then lives as a householder, keeps reciting what he learned, raises good children, turns his senses toward the Self, and harms no living being except in sacred rites, reaches the world of Brahman and is never reborn.
themes: how to live a good life

upanishads-prashna-4-3.plain: Even while a person sleeps, the breaths in the body stay awake like sacred fires kept burning in a house. The teacher Pippalada compares the different breaths (prana, the life-breaths) to the three fires used in Vedic worship.
themes: the body as a sacred place

upanishads-prashna-4-4.plain: The comparison goes on: one breath balances breathing out and in, like a priest making offerings. The mind is the one offering the worship. Another breath, the upward breath, is the reward, because each night in deep sleep it carries the mind to Brahman, the highest reality.

upanishads-prashna-4-5.plain: In dreams the mind plays freely. It sees again what it saw and hears again what it heard, even things from faraway places. It also sees things it never really saw or heard, because in dreams the mind makes up the whole world itself.

upanishads-prashna-4-6.plain: When the mind is filled with a deeper light, it stops dreaming. This is dreamless deep sleep, and in that state a peaceful happiness rises in the body.

upanishads-prashna-4-7.plain: Just as birds fly back to a tree to rest at night, everything in us goes back to rest in the highest Self, the Atman, in deep sleep.

upanishads-prashna-4-8.plain: This is the list of everything that rests in the Self in deep sleep: the elements like earth, water, fire, air and space, the senses and what they sense, the hands, feet and voice and what they do, and the mind, intellect, sense of 'I', thought, and breath, with all they handle.
themes: list of what makes us up

upanishads-prashna-4-9.plain: The one who really sees, hears, smells, tastes, thinks and acts inside us is a knowing person. That inner person lives in the highest Self, which can never be destroyed.
themes: something in me that never dies

upanishads-prashna-4-10.plain: Whoever knows this Self that cannot be destroyed reaches the highest thing. This Self has no shadow, no body and no color, and it shines. Knowing it, a person comes to know everything and becomes one with everything.

upanishads-prashna-4-11.plain: Pippalada finishes his answer to Gargya: whoever knows the undying Self, where the knower, the breaths, the senses and the elements all rest, knows everything and has reached into everything.

upanishads-prashna-5-1.plain: Next, a student named Satyakama asks the teacher: if a person meditates on the sacred sound Om for the whole of life, until death, what does that person gain?

upanishads-prashna-5-2.plain: Pippalada answers that Om stands for both the highest Brahman, which is beyond everything, and the lower form of Brahman that we can picture. So by meditating on Om, a person reaches one or the other.

upanishads-prashna-5-3.plain: Om has three sounds: A, U and M. Someone who meditates only on the first sound, A, is soon reborn on earth as a human. There, with self-discipline, self-control and faith, that person lives a great life.

upanishads-prashna-5-4.plain: Someone who meditates on the first two sounds, A and U, goes after death to a heavenly world called the Soma-world. After enjoying it for a while, that person comes back to be born again.

upanishads-prashna-5-5.plain: Someone who meditates on all three sounds of Om, thinking of the Highest Person, goes to the light of the sun. Like a snake leaving its old skin, that person is freed from wrongdoing. Carried to the world of Brahma, the creator, that person learns to see the Highest Person who is everywhere.

upanishads-prashna-5-6.plain: The three sounds of Om, used separately, lead only to things that pass away. But when they are joined and used rightly in every kind of action, outer, inner or in between, the wise person does not shake with fear.

upanishads-prashna-5-7.plain: Through the different kinds of Vedic verses, a person reaches this world, the sky, or the world the poets describe. But through Om, the wise one reaches the Highest, which is peaceful and free from aging, death and fear.

upanishads-prashna-6-1.plain: The last student, Sukesha, tells the teacher that a prince once asked him about the 'person of sixteen parts.' Sukesha honestly said he did not know, because telling a lie destroys a person to the root. The prince left in silence. Now Sukesha asks the teacher where that person is.

upanishads-prashna-6-2.plain: The teacher Pippalada replies that this person is right here inside the body. The sixteen parts all come from this person.

upanishads-prashna-6-3.plain: This inner person, before creating anything, thought: 'What is it that, when it leaves, I leave too, and when it stays, I stay?'

upanishads-prashna-6-4.plain: So this person first created prana, the life-breath. From the breath came faith, space, air, fire, water, earth, the senses, mind and food. From food came strength, self-discipline, sacred hymns, worship, the worlds, and names for everything.

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-4.plain: The passage compares the eye to the Sama chant. The bright white part of the eye stands for the Rik (a verse of the Rig Veda), and the deep dark part stands for the Saman (the sung chant). The dark rests on the bright, just as the chant is sung on top of the verse.
themes: how the body mirrors sacred things
seeing the holy in everyday things

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-5.plain: The person seen inside the eye is the same as the shining person in the sun. He is every part of the sacred chants and is Brahman, the ultimate reality. Inside and outside, the divine has the same form and the same name.
themes: is the divine inside or outside

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-6.plain: This person in the eye rules over the worlds below and over all human wishes. So whenever people sing to the vina (a stringed instrument), they are really singing to him, and he is the source of the wealth they gain.

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-7.plain: A person who understands this and sings the chant is praising both at once: the divine person in the sun and the one in the eye, as one being. Through the one in the sun, he gains the higher worlds and what the gods wish for.

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-8.plain: Through the one in the eye, he also gains this lower world and what humans wish for. So a chanting priest (Udgatri) who knows this can make an offer to the person he chants for.

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-9.plain: The priest can ask, "What wish shall I win for you with my song?" Someone who sings the chant with this knowledge can make wishes come true through singing.

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-1.plain: Three men skilled in the udgitha (the main sacred chant) were Silaka, Dalbhya and Pravahana. They agreed to sit down and discuss it together.

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-2.plain: They sat down. Pravahana, a king, politely asked the two priests to speak first, because he wanted to hear what they had to say.

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-3.plain: Silaka said to Dalbhya, "Let me ask you a question." Dalbhya told him to go ahead.

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-4.plain: Silaka asked where the chant comes from, and Dalbhya answered step by step. The chant comes from tone, tone comes from breath, breath comes from food, and food comes from water.
themes: how life depends on food and water

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-5.plain: Dalbhya said water comes from heaven. When asked where heaven comes from, he said the questioning should stop there, because the chant belongs in heaven.

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-6.plain: Silaka told Dalbhya that his answer had no firm ground. He warned that if someone had bet his head on it, Dalbhya would have lost it.

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-7.plain: Dalbhya humbly asked Silaka to teach him. Silaka said heaven comes from this world, and that the chant rests on this world, so the questioning should stop there.

upanishads-chandogya-1-8-8.plain: Then Pravahana told Silaka that his answer, the earth, also has an end, so it cannot be the final source. Silaka humbly asked Pravahana to teach him, and he agreed.

upanishads-chandogya-1-9-1.plain: Pravahana taught that this world comes from space (ether). All beings come out of space and go back into it. Space is older than everything and is where everything rests.

upanishads-chandogya-1-9-2.plain: This space is the sacred chant and the syllable Om, which stands for Brahman, the ultimate reality. It is greater than the greatest and has no end. Whoever meditates on it with this understanding gains the highest things.

upanishads-chandogya-1-9-3.plain: The teacher Atidhanvan taught this chant to his student Udara-sandilya. He promised that as long as his family kept this knowledge, their life in this world would be better and better.
themes: passing wisdom to the next generation

upanishads-chandogya-1-9-4.plain: He said the same would be true for them in the next world. Whoever knows and meditates on the chant this way will have the best life here and after death.
themes: a good life now and later

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-1.plain: After hailstorms ruined the land of the Kurus, a man named Ushasti lived as a beggar with his very young wife in a village.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-2.plain: Ushasti saw a local man eating beans and begged him for some. The man said he had no more except the beans already set out for himself.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-8.plain: Brahman, the one reality behind everything, grows through deep inner concentration, and from it comes matter, called "food" here. From matter come breath, mind, the elements, the worlds, and the deeds people do there, whose results last on and on.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-9.plain: The highest Brahman sees all and knows all, and its concentration is pure knowing. From it come the creator god (also called Brahman), along with names, shapes and matter.
themes: where names and forms come from

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-1.plain: The fire rituals that ancient poet-seers found in the Vedic hymns are real and were done in many ways in an earlier age. People who love truth should do them carefully, because they lead to a heavenly world earned by good deeds.
themes: earning a reward through good deeds

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-2.plain: When the sacred fire is lit and the flame is dancing, a person should pour in the offering at the right spot, between two portions of melted butter, and do it with faith.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-3.plain: If a person does the daily fire offering, called the Agnihotra, but skips the other required rituals, ignores guests, or does it carelessly and against the rules, it harms him instead of helping. It ruins all the good worlds he hoped to reach.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-4.plain: The sacred fire has seven flickering tongues of flame. Their names are Black, Terrible, Swift as Thought, Very Red, Smoky Purple, Sparkling, and All-Shaped.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-5.plain: If a person makes his offerings while these flames are shining and at the right times, the offerings carry him like rays of sunlight. They take him to the place where Indra, the king of the gods, lives.
themes: doing things at the right time

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-6.plain: The shining offerings call out to the worshipper, "Come here, come here!" They carry him on the sun's rays, praise him with sweet words, and tell him, "This holy heaven is yours, earned by your good deeds."

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-7.plain: But these rituals are like weak, leaky boats. They cannot carry you across for good. Foolish people who think rituals are the highest goal keep getting old and dying, over and over again.
themes: the cycle of birth and death

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-8.plain: Foolish people live in darkness but think they are wise. Proud of what they know, they wander around lost, like blind people being led by other blind people.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-9.plain: People who stay ignorant for a long time are like children who think they are happy. Those who rely only on their good deeds are driven by desires and do not see far ahead. When the heaven they earned runs out, they fall and become miserable.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-10.plain: These fools think rituals and good deeds are the best thing there is, and they know nothing higher. After enjoying their reward in heaven for a while, they are born again into this world or an even lower one.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-11.plain: But some people live simply in the forest with self-discipline and faith. They are calm and wise and live on what others give them. Free from desire, they pass through the sun to where the undying, eternal Being lives.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-12.plain: A seeker should look carefully at everything that can be earned by actions and see that none of it lasts. Then he should let go of all wanting, because something eternal cannot be earned by actions that come and go. To learn the truth, he should carry firewood as a humble gift and go to a teacher who is learned and lives fully in Brahman.

upanishads-mundaka-1-2-13.plain: When a student comes respectfully, with a calm mind not troubled by desires, the wise teacher shares the true knowledge of Brahman. Through it the student comes to know the eternal, true Being.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-1.plain: The teacher says: this is the truth, my friend. Just as thousands of sparks fly out of a blazing fire and are made of the same fire, all living beings come out of the Imperishable, the one eternal reality, and they return to it again.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-2.plain: That divine Being has no body. It is both outside and inside everything. It was never born, does not need breath or mind, is completely pure, and is higher than anything else.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-3.plain: From that Being come breath, mind, and all the senses. From it also come space, air, fire, water, and the earth that holds everything up.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-4.plain: The whole universe is like the body of this Being. The sky is its head, the sun and moon its eyes, the directions its ears, the Vedas its speech, the wind its breath, and the world its heart. The earth came from its feet. It is the inner Self of everything.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-5.plain: From this Being comes fire, with the sun as its fuel. From the moon comes rain, and from the earth come plants. A man gives seed to a woman. In this way many living beings come from the one Person, called Purusha.
themes: one source of all living things

upanishads-isha-1.plain: Everything that moves in this world belongs to God, the Lord who lives in all things as the true Self. Let go of the idea that things are yours, and then you can truly enjoy life. Do not be greedy for what belongs to someone else.

upanishads-isha-2.plain: A person may hope to live a hundred years and keep working the whole time. If they work in this spirit, seeing all as God's, their actions will not trap them. There is no other way.

upanishads-isha-3.plain: There are dark worlds, named after the Asuras, the demons, and they are wrapped in blind darkness. People who go through life only doing things, and never learn who they really are inside, go to those worlds after death.

upanishads-isha-4.plain: The Self never moves, yet it is faster than thought. The senses, called Devas or gods here, can never catch it, because it is always ahead of them. It stays still but gets ahead of everything that runs. Matarisvan, the wind or moving spirit, gives powers to it.
themes: the mind can't grasp the divine

upanishads-isha-5.plain: The Self moves and does not move. It is far away and also very close. It is inside everything and also outside everything.

upanishads-isha-6.plain: A person who sees all living beings inside the Self, and the Self inside all beings, never turns away from it and never hates anyone.

upanishads-isha-7.plain: When a wise person sees that the one Self has become everything, sorrow and confusion fall away. Once someone has seen this oneness, what can make them sad or troubled?

upanishads-isha-8.plain: The Self is everywhere. It is bright and has no body, no wounds and no muscles. It is pure and untouched by evil. It is a wise seer who exists by itself, and it has set all things in their proper order for all time.

upanishads-isha-9.plain: People who only follow rituals and good works go into blind darkness. But people who only care about knowledge and ignore their duties go into even greater darkness.

upanishads-isha-10.plain: The wise teachers said that knowledge brings one result and good works bring a different result. This is what was handed down to us.

upanishads-isha-11.plain: A person who understands both knowledge and works together uses good works to get past death, and uses true knowledge to reach immortal life.

upanishads-isha-12.plain: People who worship only the changing world go into blind darkness. People who worship only the hidden first cause of everything, and ignore the rest, go into even greater darkness.

upanishads-isha-13.plain: The wise said that knowing the first cause brings one result, and knowing the changing world brings another. This is what our teachers told us.

upanishads-isha-14.plain: A person who understands both the eternal cause and the body that dies uses the body and this life to get past death. Through knowing the true cause, they reach immortality.

upanishads-isha-15.plain: The speaker prays to Pushan, the sun god who nourishes the world. The truth is hidden behind a golden disk, like the bright sun. He asks Pushan to open it so he can see what is truly real.

upanishads-isha-16.plain: The speaker keeps praying to the sun, calling it Pushan, the one seer, Yama the judge, Surya the sun, and child of Prajapati the creator. He asks it to pull back its blinding rays so he can see its most beautiful light. Then he realizes that the person within the sun is the same as himself.

upanishads-isha-17.plain: This is a prayer at the time of death. The speaker says his breath will return to the air and the immortal spirit, and his body will become ashes. He chants Om and tells his mind to remember all the deeds he has done.

upanishads-isha-18.plain: The speaker prays to Agni, the god of fire, who knows everything. He asks Agni to lead us by a good path to the highest good and to keep crooked, evil ways far from us. In return, we will praise him with all our hearts.

upanishads-kena-1-1.plain: A student asks his teacher who makes the mind think, who starts our breathing, who makes us speak, and what god makes our eyes see and ears hear.

upanishads-kena-1-2.plain: The teacher answers that it is the power behind the ear, mind, speech, breath and eye, the thing that makes them work at all. The wise who see this and stop identifying with the senses become immortal when they leave this world.

upanishads-chandogya-3-4-2.plain: The hymns of the Atharva Veda are pictured as bees working over the old stories and histories. From this work came fame, a shining face, energy, strength and good health, like honey.
themes: where strength and health come from
a picture of the Vedas as bees

upanishads-chandogya-3-4-3.plain: This honey-like essence flowed up to the sun. It became the very dark light that can be seen in the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-3-5-1.plain: The sun's rays that point upward are the honeycomb cells at the top. The secret teachings are the bees, Brahman (here meaning the sacred sound Om) is the flower, and water is the nectar.
themes: a picture of the Vedas as bees

upanishads-chandogya-3-5-2.plain: The secret teachings worked over Om like bees over a flower. From this came fame, a shining face, brightness, energy, strength and good health.
themes: where strength and health come from

upanishads-chandogya-3-5-3.plain: This essence flowed up to the sun. It became the thing that seems to move and shimmer in the middle of the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-3-5-4.plain: The colours in the sun are the best of the best. The Vedas are the finest and most lasting things in the world, and these colours, which rise from the Vedas through sacrifice, are their finest part, the nectar of the nectar.
themes: the best part of something good

upanishads-chandogya-3-6-1.plain: The first nectar, the red light of the sun, feeds the Vasus, a group of gods led by Agni, the god of fire. The gods do not eat or drink; they are happy just by looking at the nectar.
themes: the red light of the sun

upanishads-chandogya-3-6-2.plain: The Vasus go into that red colour and come out of it again.
themes: the Vasus and the red light

upanishads-chandogya-3-6-3.plain: A person who truly understands this nectar becomes one of the Vasus, led by Agni. He sees the nectar and is happy, and he too goes into that colour and rises from it.

upanishads-chandogya-3-6-4.plain: For as long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, this person shares the rule and greatness of the Vasus.

upanishads-chandogya-3-7-1.plain: The second nectar feeds the Rudras, a group of storm gods led by Indra, king of the gods. The gods do not eat or drink; they are happy just by looking at the nectar.
themes: the white light of the sun

upanishads-chandogya-3-7-2.plain: The Rudras go into that white colour and come out of it again.
themes: the Rudras and the white light

upanishads-chandogya-3-7-3.plain: A person who truly understands this nectar becomes one of the Rudras, led by Indra. He sees the nectar and is happy, and he too goes into that colour and rises from it.

upanishads-chandogya-3-7-4.plain: The sun will later rise in the south and set in the north for twice as long as it now rises in the east. For that whole time, this person shares the rule of the Rudras.

upanishads-chandogya-3-8-1.plain: The third nectar feeds the Adityas, a group of gods led by Varuna, the god of the waters and cosmic order. The gods do not eat or drink; they are happy just by looking at the nectar.
themes: the dark light of the sun

upanishads-chandogya-3-8-2.plain: The Adityas go into that dark colour and come out of it again.
themes: the Adityas and the dark light

upanishads-chandogya-3-8-3.plain: A person who truly understands this nectar becomes one of the Adityas, led by Varuna. He sees the nectar and is happy, and he too goes into that colour and rises from it.

upanishads-chandogya-3-8-4.plain: The sun will later rise in the west and set in the east for twice as long as it rose in the south. For that whole time, this person shares the rule of the Adityas.

upanishads-chandogya-3-9-1.plain: The fourth nectar feeds the Maruts, a group of wind gods led by Soma, the god of the sacred drink and the moon. The gods do not eat or drink; they are happy just by looking at the nectar.
themes: the very dark light of the sun

upanishads-chandogya-3-9-2.plain: The Maruts go into that very dark colour and come out of it again.
themes: the Maruts and the very dark light

upanishads-chandogya-3-16-2.plain: If a person falls sick in the first part of life, his first 24 years, he can pray to his life-breaths (Prânas), which are like the Vasus, gods who keep things alive. He asks them to stretch his life on into the middle years so he does not die young. By this prayer he gets well again.

upanishads-chandogya-3-16-3.plain: The next 44 years of life are compared to the midday offering of a great ritual. The life-breaths in this stage are linked to the Rudras, storm gods, because they make people cry.
themes: hardship and tears in adult life

upanishads-chandogya-3-16-4.plain: If a person falls sick in the middle years, he can ask his life-breaths, like the Rudras, to carry his life on into old age. By this prayer he gets well again.

upanishads-chandogya-3-16-5.plain: The last 48 years of life are compared to the evening offering of the ritual. The life-breaths in this stage are linked to the Âdityas, sun gods, because they gather everything up.

upanishads-chandogya-3-16-6.plain: If a person falls sick in old age, he can ask his life-breaths, like the Âdityas, to carry his life on to its full length. By this prayer he gets well again.

upanishads-chandogya-3-16-7.plain: The sage Mahidâsa Aitareya knew this teaching. He told a sickness, "Why trouble me? I will not die from you." He lived 116 years, and the passage says anyone who knows this will live that long too.

upanishads-chandogya-3-17-1.plain: When a person goes hungry and thirsty and gives up pleasures, that is like the start of a sacred ritual. Everyday self-control is a holy act.

upanishads-chandogya-3-17-2.plain: When a person eats, drinks and enjoys life, that is like the ritual days when eating is allowed. Ordinary enjoyment can also be part of a sacred life.

upanishads-chandogya-3-17-3.plain: When a person laughs, eats and has fun, that is like singing the hymns at a ritual. Joy itself is a kind of praise.

upanishads-chandogya-3-17-4.plain: Self-discipline, generosity, doing right, kindness and truthfulness are the true gifts a person offers. These are like the gifts given to priests at a ritual.

upanishads-chandogya-3-17-5.plain: The ritual words "there will be a birth" and "there has been a birth" stand for a person's birth. His death is like the ritual's last step, when the vessels are taken away to be washed. A whole life is one big sacred ceremony.

upanishads-chandogya-3-17-6.plain: The teacher Ghora Ângirasa taught this to Krishna, son of Devaki, and after that Krishna wanted no other knowledge. Ghora said that when death comes near, a person should take comfort in three thoughts: "You are the one that never perishes," "You are the one that never changes," and "You are the finest essence of life."
themes: comfort at the end of life
the part of us that never dies

upanishads-chandogya-3-17-7.plain: Two verses from the Rig-veda are quoted. They say wise people see within themselves an ancient light that is always there. Rising above darkness, they reach the highest light, the light in the sun and in the heart.
themes: hope at the end of life

upanishads-chandogya-3-18-1.plain: A person should meditate on the mind as Brahman, the ultimate reality, when thinking about the body. He should meditate on space as Brahman when thinking about the world of the gods.

upanishads-chandogya-3-18-2.plain: Brahman, seen as mind, has four parts like four feet. In the body they are speech, breath, sight and hearing. In the outer world they are fire, air, the sun and the directions.
themes: seeing the sacred in our senses

upanishads-chandogya-3-18-3.plain: Speech is one of the four feet of Brahman, and it shines with the light of fire. Whoever knows this will shine with fame and a glowing face.

upanishads-chandogya-3-18-4.plain: Breath is one of the four feet of Brahman, and it shines with the light of the air. Whoever knows this will shine with fame and a glowing face.

upanishads-chandogya-3-18-5.plain: The eye is one of the four feet of Brahman, and it shines with the light of the sun. Whoever knows this will shine with fame and a glowing face.

upanishads-chandogya-3-18-6.plain: The ear is one of the four feet of Brahman, and it shines with the light of the directions of space. Whoever knows this will shine with fame and a glowing face.

upanishads-chandogya-3-19-1.plain: The sun should be worshipped as Brahman, the ultimate reality. In the beginning there was nothing; then something came to be and grew into an egg. After a year the egg broke into two halves, one silver and one gold.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-6.plain: Holding the herb-and-honey mash in his hands, the person doing the rite speaks to Prana, the life-breath. He calls it Ama, because everything lives within it, and praises it as the oldest, best and ruling power. He asks to become great like it.
themes: respect for the breath of life

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-7.plain: He eats the mash in small swallows, one after each line of a sacred verse. The verse praises the food of the sun god Savitri, here meaning the life-breath, as the best food that supports everything. At the last line he drinks all that is left.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-8.plain: After washing the bowl, he sits quietly behind the fire on an animal skin or the bare ground. He does not speak or do anything else. If he dreams of a woman, that is a sign the rite has worked.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-9.plain: A short verse repeats the teaching. If someone doing a rite for a wish dreams of a woman, he can take it as a sign of success.

upanishads-chandogya-5-3-1.plain: A young man named Svetaketu goes to a gathering of the Panchala people. King Pravahana Jaivali asks him if his father has taught him, and he proudly says yes.

upanishads-chandogya-5-3-2.plain: The king asks Svetaketu where people go after they die and how they come back. He also asks where the path of the gods and the path of the ancestors split apart. Svetaketu cannot answer any of these.

upanishads-chandogya-5-3-3.plain: The king asks two more questions. Why does the world beyond never fill up with the dead? Why, in the fifth offering, is water called 'man'? Svetaketu cannot answer these either.

upanishads-chandogya-5-3-4.plain: The king asks how Svetaketu could claim to be educated without knowing these things. Svetaketu goes home sad and complains to his father that he was never really taught.

upanishads-chandogya-5-3-5.plain: Svetaketu says the king, a man of the warrior class, asked him five questions and he could not answer one. His father, Gautama, honestly admits that he does not know the answers either. If he had known them, he would have taught his son.

upanishads-chandogya-5-3-6.plain: Gautama goes to the king, who welcomes him with respect. The king offers him any worldly gift, but Gautama refuses. He asks only to learn what the king told his son.

upanishads-chandogya-5-3-7.plain: The king is troubled, and he asks Gautama to stay with him for a while. He explains that this teaching had never gone to a Brahmin, a priest, before. Until now only the warrior class knew it. Then he begins to teach.

upanishads-chandogya-5-4-1.plain: The king begins by comparing heaven to a sacrificial fire. The sun is its fuel and the sun's rays are its smoke. The day is its light, the moon its glowing coals and the stars its sparks.
themes: the universe as a sacred offering

upanishads-chandogya-5-4-2.plain: Into this heavenly fire the gods (the powers of life) pour an offering of faith, in the form of water. From this offering the moon, called King Soma, is born.

upanishads-chandogya-5-5-1.plain: The second fire is Parjanya, the god of rain. The air is its fuel and the cloud its smoke. Lightning is its light, the thunderbolt its coals and the rumbling thunder its sparks.

upanishads-chandogya-5-5-2.plain: Into the rain-fire the gods offer the moon. From that offering, rain is born.

upanishads-chandogya-5-6-1.plain: The third fire is the earth. The year is its fuel and the sky its smoke. Night is its light, the four directions its coals and the in-between directions its sparks.

upanishads-chandogya-5-6-2.plain: Into the earth-fire the gods offer rain. From that offering, food such as grain is born.

upanishads-chandogya-5-7-1.plain: The fourth fire is a man. Speech is its fuel and breath its smoke. The tongue is its light, the eyes its coals and the ears its sparks.

upanishads-chandogya-5-7-2.plain: Into the man-fire the gods offer food. From that offering, seed is born.

upanishads-chandogya-5-8-1.plain: The fifth fire is a woman, the king says to Gautama.

upanishads-chandogya-2-21-1.plain: A Sāman is a chant from the Vedas, and it has five parts. Here each part is matched with something in the universe: the three Vedas (sacred books), the three worlds, the gods of fire, air and sun, the stars, birds and light rays, and the serpents, heavenly singers called Gandharvas, and the spirits of ancestors. This shows the chant as woven into everything.
themes: seeing the sacred in all things

upanishads-chandogya-2-21-2.plain: A person who understands that this chant runs through everything becomes one with everything.

upanishads-chandogya-2-21-3.plain: An old verse is quoted to support this. It says the three groups (the Vedas, the worlds and so on), each arranged in the five parts of the chant, along with the other forms of the chant, are the highest thing, and nothing is greater.

upanishads-chandogya-2-21-4.plain: Whoever knows this knows everything, and people from every direction bring him gifts. His rule is to meditate on the chant while knowing that he himself is everything.
themes: sense of who I really am

upanishads-chandogya-2-22-1.plain: The main part of the chant, the udgītha, can be sung in different tones, and each tone belongs to a different god. A deep tone belongs to Agni, god of fire; others belong to Prajāpati the creator, Soma, Vāyu the wind, Indra king of gods, and Brihaspati the gods' teacher. The dull tone belongs to Varuna, and a singer should use all the tones except that one.

upanishads-chandogya-2-22-2.plain: The priest who sings should hold good wishes in mind as he sings: life without death for the gods, offerings for the ancestors, hope for people, food and water for animals, heaven for the person paying for the ritual, and food for himself. He should also sing carefully without mistakes.

upanishads-chandogya-2-22-3.plain: The sounds of speech belong to different gods: vowels to Indra, hissing sounds like 's' to Prajāpati, and stop consonants to Mrityu, which means Death. If someone criticizes the singer's vowels, he should say he relied on Indra, and Indra will answer them.

upanishads-chandogya-2-22-4.plain: If someone criticizes the singer's hissing sounds, he should say he relied on Prajāpati, who will crush the critic. If someone criticizes his consonants, he should say he relied on Death, who will burn the critic to ashes.

upanishads-chandogya-2-22-5.plain: This explains how to pronounce the sounds. Vowels should be sung loud and strong to give strength to Indra. Hissing sounds should be clear and open, not swallowed or spat out. Consonants should be sung slowly, without running them together, so the singer keeps himself away from Death.

upanishads-chandogya-2-23-1.plain: There are three branches of religious duty. The first is doing sacred rituals, studying, and giving to others.
themes: how to live a good life

upanishads-chandogya-2-23-2.plain: The second branch is self-discipline. The third is living as a student in a teacher's home and living strictly there. All of these lead to happy heavenly worlds, but only the person firmly rooted in Brahman, the ultimate reality, reaches a life beyond death.

upanishads-chandogya-2-23-3.plain: Prajāpati, the creator, thought deeply about the worlds, and from them came the three Vedas. He thought deeply about the Vedas, and from them came three sacred words: Bhūh, Bhuvah and Svah, meaning earth, sky and heaven.

upanishads-chandogya-2-23-4.plain: Then from those three words came the sound Om. Just as all leaves are held together by their stems, all words are held together by Om. Om is everything.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-1.plain: The teachers of the Vedas say that the morning offering belongs to the Vasus, the noon offering belongs to the Rudras, and the evening offering belongs to the Ādityas and the All-Gods. These are groups of gods.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-2.plain: So if all three offerings belong to the gods, what world is left for the person making the offering? Someone who doesn't know the answer should not perform the ritual. Only someone who understands should do it.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-3.plain: Before the morning chant begins, the person making the offering sits behind the household fire altar, faces north, and sings a chant to the Vasus.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-4.plain: He sings: 'Open the door of this earth so we may see you and rule here on earth.'
themes: asking for a place in the world

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-5.plain: Then he makes the offering and says: 'Praise to Agni, the fire god who lives on earth! Win this world for me! This is my world.'

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-6.plain: He says, 'When this life is over I will go there. Take this offering! Open the door!' Then he stands up. For such a person, the Vasus complete the morning offering.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-7.plain: Before the noon offering begins, the person making the offering sits behind another altar, called the Āgnīdhrīya, faces north, and sings a chant to the Rudras.

upanishads-chandogya-4-15-1.plain: The teacher tells Upakosala that the person seen in the eye is the true Self. It cannot die and has nothing to fear, and it is Brahman, the ultimate reality. Like an eye that stays clean when butter or water drips on it, the Self is untouched by anything.

upanishads-chandogya-4-15-2.plain: The Self is called Samyadvama, meaning 'the one toward whom all good things come.' A person who understands this also has all good things come to them.

upanishads-chandogya-4-15-3.plain: The Self is also called Vamani, meaning 'the one who brings all good things.' A person who knows this also brings good things to others.

upanishads-chandogya-4-15-4.plain: The Self is also called Bhamani, meaning 'the one who shines in all worlds.' A person who knows this also shines everywhere.

upanishads-chandogya-4-15-5.plain: When a person who knows this dies, it does not matter whether funeral rites are done for them. They travel through stages of light: day, the bright half of the month, the sun's northern half-year, the year, the sun, the moon and lightning. There a being who is not human meets them.

upanishads-chandogya-4-15-6.plain: That being leads them to Brahman, the ultimate reality. This is called the path of the gods. Those who take it are not born again as humans.

upanishads-chandogya-4-16-1.plain: The wind moves and cleans everything, so it is called the sacrifice, the sacred fire ritual. The ritual has two parts: one done with the mind and one done with words.

upanishads-chandogya-4-16-2.plain: One priest, called the Brahman priest, does his part silently in his mind. The other priests do their part out loud. This verse begins to describe what happens if the silent priest speaks during a certain stretch of the morning chants.

upanishads-chandogya-4-16-3.plain: If the silent priest breaks his silence, only the spoken part of the ritual is done right and the silent part is harmed. It is like a man hopping on one foot or a cart on one wheel. The ritual is damaged, and the person paying for it ends up worse off.

upanishads-chandogya-4-16-4.plain: But if the silent priest keeps his silence during that time, both parts of the ritual are done perfectly and neither is harmed.

upanishads-chandogya-4-16-5.plain: Like a man walking on two legs or a cart rolling on two wheels, the ritual goes well. The person paying for it is better off afterward.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-1.plain: Prajapati, the creator god, thought deeply about the worlds and drew out their essence. He got fire from the earth, air from the sky, and the sun from heaven.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-2.plain: Then Prajapati thought deeply about fire, air and sun and drew out their essence. He got the three kinds of Vedic verses: Rig verses from fire, Yajur verses from air, and Sama verses from the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-3.plain: Then he thought deeply about the three Vedas, the holy scriptures, and drew out their essence. He got three sacred words: Bhuh from the Rig verses, Bhuvah from the Yajur verses, and Svah from the Sama verses.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-4.plain: If a mistake happens in the Rig Veda part of the ritual, the priest should pour an offering into the household fire, saying 'Bhuh, Svaha!' This uses the power of the Rig verses to repair the mistake.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-5.plain: If a mistake happens in the Yajur Veda part of the ritual, the priest should pour an offering into the southern fire, saying 'Bhuvah, Svaha!' This uses the power of the Yajur verses to repair the mistake.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-6.plain: If a mistake happens in the Sama Veda part of the ritual, the priest should pour an offering into the eastern offering fire, saying 'Svah, Svaha!' This uses the power of the Sama verses to repair the mistake.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-7.plain: People join metals using other materials. Gold is joined with borax, silver with gold, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, and wood with iron or leather.
themes: the right tool for the job

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-8.plain: In the same way, any break in the ritual is repaired with the three sacred words. These words hold the essence of the worlds, the gods and the Vedas. A ritual is made whole when its overseeing priest knows this.

upanishads-chandogya-4-17-9.plain: A ritual goes the right way when it has an overseeing priest who knows this. An old verse says such a priest goes wherever the ritual slips and protects everyone, like a mare protecting the riders. So people should choose a priest who truly knows this, not one who does not.

upanishads-prashna-1-4.plain: The sage Pippalada answers that Prajapati, the lord of all creatures, wanted to make living beings. He did hard spiritual practice and then made a pair: matter (rayi) and life-force (prana), so that together they could produce all creatures.

upanishads-prashna-1-5.plain: The sun stands for life-force and the moon stands for matter. Everything, both what has a shape and what has none, is a form of matter, so the body is matter.
themes: what the body is made of

upanishads-prashna-1-6.plain: When the sun rises and shines on the east, it gathers the living beings there into its rays. As it lights up every direction, above and below, it takes in all living beings.

upanishads-prashna-1-7.plain: So the sun rises as Vaishvanara, the fire that belongs to all people. It takes every form and is both life-force and fire. A verse is then quoted to show this.
themes: the sun as shared by all

upanishads-prashna-1-8.plain: The verse praises the golden sun that takes all forms and knows all things. It rises highest, shines alone, and warms us. With a thousand rays it is present everywhere and is the life of every creature.

upanishads-prashna-1-9.plain: The year is like Prajapati and has two paths, southern and northern. People who rely only on rituals and good deeds for a reward go by the southern path, the path of the ancestors, to the moon, and then are born again. That path belongs to matter.

upanishads-prashna-1-10.plain: Those who seek the true Self through discipline, self-control, faith and knowledge take the northern path to the sun. That is the deathless, safe and highest place, and from there they do not come back, because it is the final goal.

upanishads-prashna-1-11.plain: A verse describes the year-god in different ways. Some call him a father with five feet (the five seasons) and twelve shapes (the twelve months) who sends rain from high heaven. Others picture him riding a chariot with seven wheels and six spokes.
themes: different views of the same truth

upanishads-prashna-1-12.plain: The month is also like Prajapati. Its dark half, when the moon shrinks, is matter, and its bright half is life-force. So some sages do their rituals in the bright half and others in the dark half.

upanishads-prashna-1-13.plain: Day and night are also like Prajapati: day is life-force and night is matter. The teacher says that couples who make love by day waste their life-force, while making love at night is right.

upanishads-prashna-1-14.plain: Food is also like Prajapati. From food comes the seed of life, and from that seed all creatures are born.

upanishads-prashna-1-15.plain: Couples who follow this rule of Prajapati have children, and they gain the world of Brahma here, a world of happiness. But those who live with discipline, self-control and truth go further.

upanishads-prashna-1-16.plain: The pure world of Brahma, the highest reality, belongs to those who have nothing crooked in them, no lies and no tricks.

upanishads-prashna-2-1.plain: Next the student Bhargava Vaidarbhi asks the sage how many powers, or gods, hold up a living body, how many make it show itself, and which one is the greatest.
themes: which part of us matters most

upanishads-prashna-2-2.plain: The sage says these powers are space, wind, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, eyes and ears. Once they show their strength, they argue, each boasting that it alone holds up the body.

upanishads-prashna-2-3.plain: Then Prana, the breath of life and the greatest of them, tells them not to be fooled. He alone, splitting himself into five kinds of breath, holds the body together.

upanishads-prashna-2-4.plain: The others do not believe him, so Prana starts to leave the body. As he goes, all the others are pulled out too, and when he returns they all return, like bees following their queen. Now convinced, speech, mind, eyes and ears praise Prana.

upanishads-prashna-2-5.plain: They praise Prana as fire, sun, rain, Indra the mighty god, wind and earth. He is matter and he is God. He is what exists, what does not exist, and what never dies.

upanishads-prashna-2-6.plain: Just as spokes are held in the hub of a wheel, everything rests on Prana: the sacred Vedas, the rituals, the warriors and the priests.

upanishads-prashna-2-7.plain: They continue praising Prana: as the lord of creatures, you move in the womb and are born again in every new life. All creatures make offerings to you, who live together with the senses.
themes: the start of a new life

upanishads-katha-1-1-8.plain: Yama's servants warn him that a priestly guest left without food in a careless host's house brings ruin. The host loses his hopes, his wealth, his good deeds, his children and his cattle.

upanishads-katha-1-1-9.plain: Yama, the god of death, comes home and apologizes to the boy Nachiketas. Because Nachiketas waited three nights in his house without food, Yama offers him three wishes.

upanishads-katha-1-1-10.plain: For his first wish, Nachiketas asks that his father, Gautama, calm down and stop being angry with him. He wants his father to recognize him and welcome him warmly when Death sends him back home.

upanishads-katha-1-1-11.plain: Yama grants the first wish. Nachiketas's father, also called Auddalaki Aruni, will know his son and love him as before. He will sleep peacefully, free of anger, once he sees his son come back alive from death.

upanishads-katha-1-1-12.plain: Nachiketas describes heaven. There is no fear there, no death and no worry about growing old. People there are free of hunger, thirst and sorrow, and they are happy.
themes: longing for a life without sorrow

upanishads-katha-1-1-13.plain: For his second wish, Nachiketas asks Death to teach him the fire ritual that leads to heaven. He says he truly has faith. He has heard that those in heaven do not die.

upanishads-katha-1-1-14.plain: Yama agrees to teach the fire ritual. He tells Nachiketas that understanding it leads to endless worlds. It is their firm foundation, though it is hidden and hard to see.

upanishads-katha-1-1-15.plain: Yama explains the fire ritual: what bricks to use for the altar, how many, and how to lay them. Nachiketas repeats it all back correctly. This pleases Death, also called Mrityu.
themes: a teacher pleased with a student

upanishads-katha-1-1-16.plain: Pleased, the generous Yama gives Nachiketas an extra gift. The fire ritual will be named after him, and he also receives a colorful necklace.

upanishads-katha-1-1-17.plain: Yama says that a person who does this Nachiketas ritual three times rises above birth and death. That person must also stay close to father, mother and teacher, and do three duties: study, worship and giving to others. Whoever truly understands this sacred fire finds lasting peace.

upanishads-katha-1-1-18.plain: Yama says that whoever knows and performs the threefold Nachiketas fire ritual breaks free from death's grip. That person is happy in heaven, beyond the reach of grief.

upanishads-katha-1-1-19.plain: Yama tells Nachiketas that this heaven-leading fire is now his, as his second wish. People everywhere will call it by his name. Then Yama asks him to choose his third wish.

upanishads-katha-1-1-20.plain: For his third wish, Nachiketas asks what happens when a person dies. Some say the person still exists and others say they do not. He wants Death himself to teach him the truth.

upanishads-katha-1-1-21.plain: Death tries to avoid the question. He says even the gods once doubted this and it is very hard to understand. He asks Nachiketas to pick a different wish.
themes: being told to drop a question

upanishads-katha-1-1-22.plain: Nachiketas refuses to back down. If even the gods were unsure, and if no teacher could explain it better than Death himself, then no other wish could be as valuable.
themes: not giving up on the truth

upanishads-katha-1-1-23.plain: Death tries to tempt Nachiketas with other gifts. He offers children and grandchildren who live a hundred years, cattle, elephants, gold, horses, a great kingdom, and as long a life as he wants.

upanishads-katha-1-1-24.plain: Death keeps offering. Nachiketas can have wealth and long life, rule the whole earth, and enjoy everything he desires, if only he picks something else.

upanishads-katha-1-1-25.plain: Death offers even rare pleasures no human can get, like beautiful women with chariots and music to serve him. He only asks that Nachiketas stop asking about death.

upanishads-katha-1-1-26.plain: Nachiketas answers that these pleasures only last a short while and they wear out a person's strength. Even a whole lifetime is short. He tells Death to keep his horses, dancing and songs.

upanishads-katha-1-1-27.plain: Nachiketas says money cannot make anyone truly happy. Riches mean little when death is always coming. He will only accept the wish he already chose: to know what happens after death.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-6.plain: Everything to do with worship comes from the one Person, the source of all. This includes the sacred hymns of the Vedas (the Rik, Saman and Yajus), the rites that start a person's religious life, all sacrifices, and the gifts paid to priests. The year, the worshipper, and the worlds lit by the sun and moon come from him too.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-7.plain: The gods, spirits, people, animals and birds all come from this one source. So do breathing, food grains, self-discipline, faith, truth, self-control and moral law.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-8.plain: Our senses also come from him. So do the act of sensing, the things we sense, and what we experience through them. They are counted in groups of seven and rest in the hidden space of the heart.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-9.plain: The seas, mountains and rivers all come from him. So do the plants and the sap that feeds the body, which keeps the inner Self living in it.

upanishads-mundaka-2-1-10.plain: The divine Person is all of this: worship, discipline, and Brahman, the highest reality that never dies. Whoever finds him hidden in their own heart is freed, even in this life, from the tangle of not knowing the truth.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-1.plain: The great Being is close to us and plain to see. It lives in the hidden space of the heart. Everything that moves, breathes or blinks rests in it, and so does everything that exists or does not. It is worthy of worship, the very best, and beyond what our minds can grasp.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-2.plain: Brahman, the ultimate reality, is shining and smaller than the smallest thing. Yet all the worlds and everyone in them rest on it. It cannot be destroyed. It is the life-breath, speech and mind, and it is true and immortal. The teacher tells his student: aim at it and hit it.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-3.plain: The teaching is like a mighty bow. Put on it an arrow made sharp by devotion. Then draw it back with your mind fixed on what is real, and hit the target, which is the Indestructible.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-4.plain: The sacred sound Om is the bow, your own Self is the arrow, and Brahman is the target. A person who is careful and alert can hit it. Then, just as an arrow sinks into its target, they become one with Brahman.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-5.plain: Heaven, earth, sky, the mind and all the senses are woven together in him. Know him alone as your true Self and stop the empty talk. He is the bridge that leads to immortality.
themes: too much talk, not enough practice

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-6.plain: The Self lives in the heart, where the body's channels meet like spokes in the center of a wheel, and it shows up in many forms. Meditate on the Self using the sound Om. The teacher wishes you well as you cross over the darkness.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-7.plain: The Self knows and understands everything, and all the glory of the world is his. He lives in the space of the heart, called Brahman's city. He takes the form of the mind, guides the body and senses, and is kept alive by food near the heart. Wise people who understand this see the immortal one shining with joy.
themes: the heart as a sacred place

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-8.plain: When a person truly sees the One who is both the highest and the lowest, the cause and all its results, the knots in their heart come undone. All their doubts are cleared up, and their past actions lose their hold on them.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-9.plain: In the innermost golden layer of a person is Brahman. It is pure and whole, without desires and without parts. It is the light of all lights, and those who know the Self know it.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-10.plain: There, the sun, moon, stars, lightning and fire do not shine on their own. When Brahman shines, everything else shines after it. All things get their light from its light.

upanishads-mundaka-2-2-11.plain: The immortal Brahman is in front, behind, to the right and to the left. It spreads below and above. Brahman alone is everything, and it is the best.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-1.plain: Two birds, close friends that are never apart, sit on the same tree. One eats the sweet fruit. The other just watches without eating.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-2.plain: A person sits on that same tree, sunk in sorrow and confused, feeling powerless. But when they see the other bird, the Lord, calm and content, and see his greatness, their sorrow goes away.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-3.plain: When a person sees the shining Creator and Lord, whose source is Brahman, that person becomes wise. They rise above good and bad deeds, become free of cravings, and reach the highest oneness.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-4.plain: The Lord is the life-breath shining in every being. Whoever understands this becomes truly wise, not just someone who talks about it. They find joy and delight in the Self. After doing their duties, such as being truthful, disciplined and meditating, they rest firmly in Brahman as the best of those who know it.

upanishads-chandogya-6-7-2.plain: Svetaketu goes without food for fifteen days, as his father told him. When his father asks him to recite the Vedas, the holy verses he had learned (the Rik, Yajus and Saman), he says he cannot remember them.

upanishads-chandogya-6-7-3.plain: His father explains with a picture. When a big fire burns down, only one tiny coal, as small as a firefly, is left. In the same way, only one of Svetaketu's sixteen parts is left, so he cannot remember the Vedas. The father tells him to go and eat.
themes: why I can't think when hungry

upanishads-chandogya-6-7-4.plain: The father promises Svetaketu he will understand after he eats. Svetaketu eats, comes back, and now he can answer every question and recite everything by heart.

upanishads-chandogya-6-7-5.plain: The father says that a tiny leftover coal can blaze up again if you put grass on it, and then it burns brightly.

upanishads-chandogya-6-7-6.plain: The father explains that Svetaketu's one remaining part was fed by food and blazed up again, so he could remember the Vedas. Now Svetaketu truly understands his father's teaching: the mind comes from food, breath from water, and speech from fire.

upanishads-chandogya-6-8-1.plain: Uddalaka Aruni teaches his son what deep sleep really is. When a person sleeps deeply, he is joined with the True, the real Being, and goes back to his own Self. That is why the word for sleeping, svapiti, means 'gone to one's own.'

upanishads-chandogya-6-8-2.plain: A bird tied by a string flies everywhere, finds no rest, and finally settles at the spot where it is tied. In the same way, the mind runs in every direction, finds no rest, and finally settles on the breath, because the mind is tied to the breath.

upanishads-chandogya-6-8-3.plain: The father explains hunger: when we are hungry, it is because water has digested and carried away the food we ate. So water is called the 'leader of food.' He says the body grows from food, and the body must have a deeper cause, like a sprout has a root.

upanishads-chandogya-6-8-4.plain: The body's root is food, food's root is water, water's root is fire, and fire's root is the True. All living beings come from the True, live in it, and rest in it.

upanishads-chandogya-6-8-5.plain: The father explains thirst: when we are thirsty, it is because heat (fire) has used up the water we drank. So fire is called the 'leader of water.' The body also grows from water, and it must have a deeper root.

upanishads-chandogya-6-8-6.plain: Water's root is fire, and fire's root is the True; all beings come from, live in, and rest in the True. When a person dies, his speech goes into his mind, his mind into his breath, his breath into heat, and heat into the Highest Being.

upanishads-chandogya-6-8-7.plain: The father says there is one fine, hidden essence that is the true self of everything that exists. It is the True, it is the Self, and 'you are that, Svetaketu.' Svetaketu asks to learn more, and his father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-9-1.plain: The father says that bees make honey by collecting juice from many different trees and mixing it into one thing.

upanishads-chandogya-6-9-2.plain: In honey, the juices cannot say which tree they came from. In the same way, when living beings merge with the True, in deep sleep or in death, they do not know that they have merged with it.

upanishads-chandogya-6-9-3.plain: Whatever creatures are here, whether a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, or a mosquito, they come back as that again and again.

upanishads-chandogya-6-9-4.plain: The father repeats: one fine, hidden essence is the true self of everything. It is the True, it is the Self, and 'you are that, Svetaketu.' Svetaketu asks to learn more, and his father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-10-1.plain: The father points out that rivers like the Ganga flow east and the Sindhu (Indus) flows west. Their water rises from the sea as clouds, falls as rain, and returns to the sea. In the sea, the rivers no longer know 'I am this river' or 'that river.'

upanishads-chandogya-6-10-2.plain: In the same way, living beings come out of the True without knowing they came from it. Whatever they are, whether a lion, a wolf, a worm, or a mosquito, they become that again and again.

upanishads-chandogya-6-10-3.plain: The father repeats: one fine, hidden essence is the true self of everything. It is the True, it is the Self, and 'you are that, Svetaketu.' Svetaketu asks to learn more, and his father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-11-1.plain: The father says that if someone cuts a big tree at its root, trunk, or top, sap flows out like blood, but the tree stays alive. Because the living Self fills the tree, it stands strong, drinks in its food, and is happy.

upanishads-katha-2-3-7.plain: Death, the teacher, lists layers from outer to inner. The mind is deeper than the senses. Deeper than the mind is the first created Being, then the Great Self, and deeper still is the Undeveloped, the hidden root of the world.
themes: what is deeper than my thoughts

upanishads-katha-2-3-8.plain: Beyond even the Undeveloped is the Person, the true Self. It is everywhere, yet no one can see it. Anyone who comes to know this Self is set free and does not die.

upanishads-katha-2-3-9.plain: No one can see the Self with their eyes, because it has no form. It is grasped through the heart, through wisdom and through the mind. Those who know it become immortal.

upanishads-katha-2-3-10.plain: The highest state comes when the five senses and the mind are completely still. Even the thinking mind stops moving.

upanishads-katha-2-3-11.plain: Holding the senses firmly in check is what Yoga means. A person must stay alert and careful, because this calm state can come and then slip away.

upanishads-katha-2-3-12.plain: The Self cannot be reached by words, by thinking or by seeing. It can only be grasped by someone who firmly accepts that it exists.

upanishads-katha-2-3-13.plain: A person first grasps the Self by accepting that it is real. That means accepting both the unseen Brahman, the ultimate reality, and the visible world that comes from it. Once a person accepts this, the Self's true nature becomes clear to them.
themes: how to begin a spiritual path
seeing the sacred in the world

upanishads-katha-2-3-14.plain: When all the cravings in a person's heart come to an end, that mortal person becomes immortal. They reach Brahman, the ultimate reality.

upanishads-katha-2-3-15.plain: When every knot that binds the heart is cut, even while living here on earth, the mortal becomes immortal. This is the whole of the teaching.

upanishads-katha-2-3-16.plain: The heart has a hundred and one channels, and one of them goes up to the top of the head. A person who leaves the body through that channel at death reaches immortality. The other channels lead in other directions.

upanishads-katha-2-3-17.plain: The inner Self, said to be no bigger than a thumb, always lives in the human heart. A person should patiently separate this Self from the body in their understanding, the way one pulls the soft inner stalk out of a reed. They should know it as shining and undying.
themes: I am more than my body

upanishads-katha-2-3-18.plain: Nachiketa, the boy who had questioned Death, received this knowledge and the whole practice of meditation. He became free from desire and death and reached Brahman. Anyone else who understands the Self this way will reach the same goal.

upanishads-katha-2-3-19.plain: This is a closing prayer for teacher and student together. They ask God to protect them both, to give them strength, to make their learning bright, and to keep them from quarreling. It ends with Om and a wish for peace three times.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-1.plain: Brahma, the first of the gods and the maker and keeper of the world, taught the knowledge of Brahman, the ultimate reality, to his eldest son Atharva. This knowledge is the base of all other knowledge.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-2.plain: Atharvan passed this knowledge to Angir. Angir taught it to Satyavaha Bharadvaja, who then passed it on to Angiras. It was handed down from teacher to student.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-3.plain: Shaunaka, a wealthy householder, came respectfully to the teacher Angiras with a question. He asked what one thing, once known, would make everything else known.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-4.plain: Angiras answered that there are two kinds of knowledge to learn, a higher one and a lower one. Everyone who knows Brahman, the ultimate reality, says so.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-5.plain: Angiras says the lower knowledge is the four Vedas, the sacred texts, plus the studies that go with them: pronunciation, ritual, grammar, word origins, poetic meter and astronomy. The higher knowledge is the one that lets you know the Indestructible, Brahman.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-6.plain: The wise see the source of all beings as something that cannot be seen or grabbed. It has no family and no caste, no eyes, ears, hands or feet. It is eternal, everywhere, extremely subtle and never destroyed.

upanishads-mundaka-1-1-7.plain: A spider spins out its thread and takes it back in. Plants grow from the earth, and hair grows on a person's body. In the same natural way, everything in the world comes out of the Indestructible, Brahman.

upanishads-chandogya-5-22-1.plain: The teaching treats eating as a sacred fire offering. The fourth bite of food is offered to Samana, the breath that digests food and spreads it through the body, with the word "Svaha" (a call said when making an offering). Then that breath is satisfied.

upanishads-chandogya-5-22-2.plain: When the digesting breath is satisfied, the mind is satisfied. Then Parjanya, the god of rain, is satisfied, and then lightning, and then everything under them. Through all of this, the one who eats is blessed with children, cattle, health, a bright glow, and the radiance of sacred learning.

upanishads-chandogya-5-23-1.plain: The fifth bite of food is offered to Udana, the upward breath, with the word "Svaha." Then that breath is satisfied.

upanishads-chandogya-5-23-2.plain: When the upward breath is satisfied, the wind is satisfied. Then the sky or open space is satisfied, and so is everything under them. Through this, the one who eats is blessed with children, cattle, health, a bright glow, and sacred learning.

upanishads-chandogya-5-24-1.plain: If someone performs the Agnihotra, the daily fire offering, without understanding its meaning, it is useless. It is like pushing away the burning coals and pouring the offering onto cold ashes.

upanishads-chandogya-5-24-2.plain: But someone who makes this offering while truly understanding it is feeding all worlds, all beings, and all selves when they eat.

upanishads-chandogya-5-24-3.plain: Soft reed fibers burn up at once when thrown into a fire. In the same way, all the wrongs of a person are burned away when they make this offering with full understanding.

upanishads-chandogya-5-24-4.plain: Such a person, even if they give leftover food to a Chandala (a person society treated as an outcast), is really making an offering to the universal Self living in that person. A verse says that all beings gather around this offering like hungry children around their mother.

upanishads-chandogya-6-1-1.plain: There once was a boy named Shvetaketu. His father, Uddalaka, told him to go and study the Vedas, the sacred texts. He said no one in their family had ever been a priest by birth alone without truly learning.

upanishads-chandogya-6-1-2.plain: Shvetaketu began studying with a teacher at age twelve and came home at twenty-four. He had learned all the Vedas, but he came back proud, thinking he knew everything, and acting stiff and serious.

upanishads-chandogya-6-1-3.plain: His father gently asks him: since you are so proud of your learning, did you ever ask about the one teaching that lets you hear what cannot be heard, see what cannot be seen, and know what cannot be known?

upanishads-chandogya-6-1-4.plain: Shvetaketu asks what that teaching is. His father explains: if you know one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. Pots and bowls have different names, but they are all really just clay.

upanishads-chandogya-6-1-5.plain: The father gives another example. If you know one piece of gold, you know everything made of gold. Rings and necklaces are just different names. They are all really gold.

upanishads-chandogya-6-1-6.plain: In the same way, if you know one pair of iron nail clippers, you know everything made of iron, because all of it is really iron. The father says the teaching he means works like this: knowing the one source lets you know everything.

upanishads-chandogya-6-1-7.plain: Shvetaketu says his teachers must not have known this, or they would have taught him. He asks his father to teach him, and his father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-2-1.plain: The father begins: in the beginning there was only Being, one thing with nothing else beside it. He notes that some people say there was only nothing at first, and that being came out of nothing.

upanishads-chandogya-6-2-2.plain: The father rejects that view. How could something come out of nothing? No, he says, in the beginning there was only Being, one, with no second.

upanishads-chandogya-6-2-3.plain: That one Being wished to become many, and it produced fire, or heat. Heat wished to become many and produced water. That is why a hot person sweats: water comes from heat.

upanishads-chandogya-6-2-4.plain: Water wished to become many and produced earth, which means food. That is why plenty of food grows wherever it rains: food comes from water.

upanishads-chandogya-6-3-1.plain: The father says all living things come from just three kinds of birth. Some hatch from eggs, some are born from a living parent, and some sprout from a seed.

upanishads-kena-1-3.plain: The teacher says our eyes, words and thoughts cannot reach this deepest reality. We do not even know how anyone could teach it.

upanishads-kena-1-4.plain: This reality is different from everything we know, and it is also beyond what we don't know. The teacher says this is what the wise teachers of long ago passed down.

upanishads-kena-1-5.plain: Brahman, the ultimate reality, cannot be described in words, yet it is what makes speaking possible. The teacher says that alone is Brahman, not the things people usually worship here.

upanishads-kena-1-6.plain: The mind cannot think Brahman, yet Brahman is what lets the mind think at all. That alone is Brahman, not the things people usually worship.

upanishads-kena-1-7.plain: The eye cannot see Brahman, yet Brahman is what lets us see. That alone is Brahman, not the things people usually worship.

upanishads-kena-1-8.plain: The ear cannot hear Brahman, yet Brahman is what lets the ear hear. That alone is Brahman, not the things people usually worship.

upanishads-kena-1-9.plain: Brahman does not breathe with breath, yet Brahman is what makes breathing happen. That alone is Brahman, not the things people usually worship.

upanishads-kena-2-1.plain: The teacher warns the pupil: if you think you know Brahman well, you really know very little. What you know is only a small form of it.

upanishads-kena-2-2.plain: The pupil answers that he does not think he knows Brahman well, but he also cannot say he doesn't know it. Whoever understands this puzzle truly knows it.

upanishads-kena-2-3.plain: The one who admits Brahman is beyond thought really understands it. The one who thinks he has figured it out does not know it.

upanishads-kena-2-4.plain: Brahman is known in a kind of waking up, and through that we gain a life that never dies. The true Self gives us strength, and this knowing gives us immortality.

upanishads-kena-2-5.plain: Knowing Brahman in this life is the true goal of living. If you don't, you face great loss and must be born again and again, but the wise who see the Self in all things become immortal after death.

upanishads-kena-3-1.plain: Brahman won a victory for the Devas, the gods. But the gods became proud and thought the victory and greatness were all their own.

upanishads-kena-3-2.plain: Brahman saw their pride and appeared before them. The gods did not recognise it and asked, 'What strange spirit is this?'

upanishads-kena-3-3.plain: The gods asked Agni, the god of fire, also called Jatavedas (the all-knowing), to find out what this spirit was. He agreed.

upanishads-kena-3-4.plain: Agni rushed toward the spirit, and Brahman asked who he was. Agni proudly gave his names: 'I am Agni, I am Jatavedas.'

upanishads-kena-3-5.plain: Brahman asked Agni what power he had. Agni boasted that he could burn everything on earth.

upanishads-kena-3-6.plain: Brahman put a single straw in front of Agni and told him to burn it. Agni tried with all his strength but could not, so he went back and said he could not find out what the spirit was.

upanishads-kena-3-7.plain: Next the gods asked Vayu, the god of wind, to find out what the spirit was. He agreed.

upanishads-kena-3-8.plain: Vayu rushed toward the spirit, and Brahman asked who he was. Vayu proudly answered, 'I am Vayu, I am Matarisvan,' another name meaning the one who moves through the sky.

upanishads-prashna-2-8.plain: This verse continues a hymn of praise to Prana, the life-breath that keeps every living thing alive. It says Prana is what carries offerings to the gods and to the ancestors. It is also the real power behind the work of the ancient seers, the Atharvangiras.

upanishads-prashna-2-9.plain: The hymn praises Prana, the life-breath, as Indra, king of the gods, because of its brightness. It calls Prana Rudra, a fierce protecting god. It is also the sun, which moves across the sky and is the greatest of all lights.

upanishads-prashna-2-10.plain: When Prana, the life-force, sends down rain, all living creatures are happy. They hope there will be plenty of food for everyone.

upanishads-prashna-2-11.plain: The hymn calls Prana pure in itself, needing no ritual to be made holy. It names Prana the one great seer, the one who takes in everything, and the good lord. The worshippers say they give Prana its food, and they call Prana, here named Matarisvan (the wind), their father.

upanishads-prashna-2-12.plain: The worshippers pray to Prana, the life-breath that lives in our speech, hearing, sight and mind. They ask it to be kind to them and not to leave the body.

upanishads-prashna-2-13.plain: The hymn ends by saying that everything in all the worlds is under the power of Prana, the life-force. The worshippers ask it to protect them as a mother protects her children, and to give them happiness and wisdom.

upanishads-prashna-3-1.plain: A student named Kausalya Asvalayana asks the teacher about Prana, the life-force. Where does it come from? How does it enter the body, divide itself up, live there, and leave? And how does it hold up both the outer world and the inner one?

upanishads-prashna-3-2.plain: The teacher, the sage Pippalada, says these questions are even harder than the last ones. But because the student loves Brahman, the ultimate reality, he agrees to answer.

upanishads-prashna-3-3.plain: The teacher says Prana, the life-force, comes from the Self, the deepest reality. It follows the Self the way a shadow follows a person. It enters the body because of the mind's past thoughts and actions.

upanishads-prashna-3-4.plain: The main life-force works like a king. A king puts officials in charge of different villages. In the same way, Prana gives each of the other breaths in the body its own job.

upanishads-prashna-3-5.plain: The teacher names some of the breaths and where they work. Apana, the downward breath, works in the organs of waste and of making children.
