The main Prana lives in the eyes and ears and moves through the mouth and nose. Samana, the middle breath, spreads food evenly through the body, and the seven openings of the head, which let us sense the world, get their power from it.

upanishads-prashna-3-6.plain: The Self lives in the heart. From the heart spread 101 main channels, each with a hundred smaller branches, and each of those with 72,000 more. Vyana, the breath that moves all through the body, travels in these channels.
themes: the soul lives in the heart

upanishads-prashna-3-7.plain: Through one special channel, Udana, the upward breath, carries a person out at death. Good deeds lead to a good world and bad deeds to a bad world. A mix of both leads back to being born as a human.

upanishads-prashna-3-8.plain: The breaths inside us match powers in nature. The sun is the outer Prana and helps our eyes see. The earth's power supports the downward breath. The space between earth and sky matches Samana, the middle breath, and the air matches Vyana, the breath that moves all through us.

upanishads-prashna-3-9.plain: Udana, the upward breath, is linked to the body's warmth and light. When a person's inner warmth goes out at death, their senses pull back into the mind, and they move on to a new birth.

upanishads-prashna-3-10.plain: Whatever a person is thinking at the moment of death, they carry that with them into Prana, the life-force. Prana, joined with the body's warmth and with the individual soul, then leads them to the world they have earned.
themes: thoughts at the time of death

upanishads-prashna-3-11.plain: The teacher says that whoever truly understands Prana in this way will have a family line that does not die out, and will himself become immortal. He then quotes a verse to sum it up.

upanishads-prashna-3-12.plain: The verse says that whoever understands five things about Prana gains immortality. These are where it comes from, how it enters the body, where it lives, how it divides into five breaths, and how it works inside us.

upanishads-prashna-4-1.plain: Another student, Sauryayanin Gargya, asks the teacher about sleep and dreams. What in a person sleeps, and what stays awake? What power sees dreams? Who feels the happiness of deep sleep, and what does it all rest on?

upanishads-prashna-4-2.plain: The teacher explains with a picture of the sun. When it sets, all its rays gather back into it, and when it rises, they shine out again. In the same way, during sleep all the senses gather into the mind, so the person does not see, hear, speak, move or feel, and we say he is asleep.
themes: how the mind and senses work

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-5.plain: Two wise men, Saunaka Kapeya and Abhipratarin, were being served a meal. A young religious student came and asked them for food, but they gave him nothing.

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-6.plain: The student answers with a riddle. He says one hidden god, the protector of the world, swallows four great things, and people cannot see him even though he lives in many places. He adds that the food really belongs to that god, yet they have not shared it with him.

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-7.plain: Saunaka thinks about the riddle and answers the student. He says this Being is the life-force of the gods, the maker of all creatures, the great eater, who eats everything but is never eaten. He says, 'This is the One we meditate on,' and then tells the servants to give the student food.

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-8.plain: They gave the student food. The passage explains the riddle: air eats fire, sun, moon and water, and breath eats speech, sight, hearing and mind. Together these make ten, a lucky winning number in a dice game, so whoever understands this sees everything and always has food to eat.

upanishads-chandogya-4-4-1.plain: A boy named Satyakama, son of a woman named Jabala, tells his mother he wants to become a religious student. He asks her which family he comes from.
themes: questions about where I come from

upanishads-chandogya-4-4-2.plain: His mother says she does not know who his father's family is. She worked as a servant moving among many guests when she was young and became pregnant then. She tells him to call himself Satyakama Jabala, using her name.
themes: a parent telling the hard truth

upanishads-chandogya-4-4-3.plain: Satyakama goes to a teacher named Gautama Haridrumata. He politely asks if he may live and study with him.

upanishads-chandogya-4-4-4.plain: The teacher asks about his family. Satyakama does not hide anything. He repeats exactly what his mother told him and says his name is Satyakama Jabala.
themes: telling the truth when it is embarrassing

upanishads-chandogya-4-4-5.plain: The teacher says only a true Brahmin (a person of real spiritual worth) would speak so honestly, and he accepts Satyakama as a student. He gives him 400 thin, weak cows to look after. Satyakama promises himself not to come back until they become a thousand, and he lives in the forest for years caring for them.
themes: worth comes from character, not birth

upanishads-chandogya-4-5-1.plain: When the herd reached a thousand, the bull of the herd spoke to Satyakama by name. It told him the herd was now complete and asked him to lead them back to the teacher's house.

upanishads-chandogya-4-5-2.plain: The bull offers to teach Satyakama one part of Brahman (the ultimate reality behind everything). It says the four directions, east, west, south and north, make up this part, which is called 'Full of Splendour.'

upanishads-chandogya-4-5-3.plain: The bull says whoever understands this and meditates on Brahman as the four directions becomes bright and admired in this life, and wins bright worlds after it.

upanishads-chandogya-4-6-1.plain: The bull says Agni, the fire, will teach him the next part. The next day Satyakama drives the cows on. In the evening he makes a fire, pens the cows, and sits by the fire facing east.

upanishads-chandogya-4-6-2.plain: The fire calls out to Satyakama by name, and he answers respectfully, 'Sir.'

upanishads-chandogya-4-6-3.plain: The fire teaches him another part of Brahman. It is made of four things: the earth, the sky, heaven, and the ocean. This part is called 'Endless.'

upanishads-chandogya-4-6-4.plain: The fire says whoever understands this and meditates on Brahman as earth, sky, heaven and ocean becomes endless in this life and wins endless worlds.

upanishads-chandogya-4-7-1.plain: The fire says a swan-like bird will teach him the next part. The next day Satyakama drives the cows on, and in the evening again makes a fire, pens the cows, and sits facing east.

upanishads-chandogya-4-7-2.plain: A swan flies close and calls Satyakama by name. He answers, 'Sir.'

upanishads-chandogya-4-7-3.plain: The swan teaches him another part of Brahman. It is made of four lights: fire, the sun, the moon, and lightning. This part is called 'Full of Light.'
themes: God in the sun and moon

upanishads-chandogya-4-7-4.plain: The swan says whoever understands this and meditates on Brahman as these four lights becomes full of light in this life and wins worlds full of light.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-9.plain: The teacher says that a person who has found the true Self in the heart gets whatever he wishes for. If he wants loving company, it comes to him just by wishing. Whatever he truly longs for comes to him, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-3-1.plain: Our true wishes are real, but they are covered over by false things. That is why, when someone we love dies, we feel we can never see them again.

upanishads-chandogya-8-3-2.plain: Everything we long for, including loved ones who are alive or have died, can be found in our own heart, where Brahman (the ultimate reality) lives. People are like strangers walking over buried gold without knowing it. Every night in deep sleep we go into Brahman, but we do not notice, because false ideas pull us away.

upanishads-chandogya-8-3-3.plain: The Self lives in the heart. Even the Sanskrit word for heart, hridayam, is explained as meaning 'He is in the heart.' A person who knows this goes into Brahman, a kind of heaven, each night in deep sleep.

upanishads-chandogya-8-3-4.plain: The teacher says the calm being that rises from the body and shows its true form in the highest light of self-knowledge is the Self. It is deathless and without fear. It is Brahman, and its name is Satyam, which means 'the True.'

upanishads-chandogya-8-3-5.plain: The word Satyam is split into three parts. 'Sat' means what never dies, 't' means what dies, and 'yam' ties the two together. A person who understands this goes into heaven each day.

upanishads-chandogya-8-4-1.plain: The Self is like a riverbank or a dam that keeps the worlds in order. Day and night, old age, death, sadness, and even good and bad deeds cannot cross over it. Evil cannot reach it, because the world of Brahman is free from all evil.

upanishads-chandogya-8-4-2.plain: Once someone crosses over to the Self, the blind is no longer blind, the wounded is no longer wounded, and the suffering one no longer suffers. For that person night turns into day, because the world of Brahman is always full of light.

upanishads-chandogya-8-4-3.plain: The world of Brahman belongs only to those who reach it through self-control, here called brahmacharya, the disciplined life of a student. Such people are free everywhere.

upanishads-chandogya-8-5-1.plain: What people call religious sacrifice is really self-discipline, or brahmacharya. Through disciplined living, a wise person reaches what others hope to gain by rituals, and finds the Self.

upanishads-chandogya-8-5-2.plain: Long sacrifices and the vow of silence are also really self-discipline. By disciplined living a person finds safety in the True, and one who has found the Self through it truly meditates.

upanishads-chandogya-8-5-3.plain: Fasting and living as a forest hermit are also really self-discipline, and the Self found this way never dies. The passage then describes the world of Brahman: two lakes named Ara and Nya, another lake, a tree dripping Soma (a sacred drink), a city that cannot be conquered, and a golden hall. That world belongs to those who reach it through self-discipline, and they are free everywhere.

upanishads-chandogya-8-6-1.plain: The tiny channels of the heart are filled with brown, white, blue, yellow, and red substance. The sun has these same colors.

upanishads-chandogya-8-6-2.plain: Like a long road that reaches two towns, one at each end, the sun's rays reach both this world and the other. They go from the sun into the heart's channels and from those channels back to the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-8-6-3.plain: When a person sleeps deeply and peacefully without dreaming, he has entered those heart channels. Then nothing bad can touch him, because he has reached the sun's light.

upanishads-chandogya-8-6-4.plain: When a man is very ill, the people sitting around him ask, 'Do you know me? Do you know me?' As long as he has not left his body, he recognizes them.
themes: sitting with a dying loved one

upanishads-chandogya-8-6-5.plain: When a person dies, he goes upward along the sun's rays, or leaves while meditating on Om and so reaches Brahman's world. The sun is the door to that world: those who know go in, and those who do not are shut out. A verse says one of the heart's 101 channels goes up to the top of the head, and leaving by it leads to immortality.

upanishads-chandogya-8-7-1.plain: Prajapati, the creator, says we must seek and understand the Self. It has no sin, no old age, no death, no sorrow, no hunger or thirst. It wants and imagines only what is right. Whoever finds and understands it gains all worlds and all wishes.

upanishads-chandogya-8-7-2.plain: The gods and the demons both heard this and decided to look for that Self. Indra, king of the gods, and Virochana, king of the demons, each went to Prajapati separately. They carried firewood in their hands, as students did when coming to a teacher.

upanishads-chandogya-8-7-3.plain: Indra and Virochana lived with Prajapati as students for thirty-two years. When he asked why they came, they repeated his teaching about the Self and said they wanted it. Prajapati told them that the person seen in the eye is the Self, deathless and fearless. When they asked about the person seen in water or a mirror, he said it is the same one seen in all of them.

upanishads-prashna-6-5.plain: The sage Pippalada explains that rivers lose their separate names when they flow into the ocean, and people then speak only of the ocean. In the same way, the sixteen parts that make up a person (breath, senses, mind and the rest) merge back into the true Self, called the purusha. Then only that Self remains, whole and undying.

upanishads-prashna-6-6.plain: Pippalada says that all the parts of a person rest in the true Self, like the spokes of a wheel meet in its hub. Know this Self, so that death cannot harm you.

upanishads-prashna-6-7.plain: The sage Pippalada tells his students that this is all he knows about Brahman, the highest reality. There is nothing higher than it.

upanishads-prashna-6-8.plain: The students praise Pippalada. They tell him he is like a father to them, because he carried them across from not knowing to true understanding, like a boat taking them to the far shore.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-1.plain: A person should meditate on the sacred syllable Om. It is also called the udgitha, a chant from the Sama Veda (a book of sacred hymns), because that chant begins with Om. The full explanation of Om follows.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-2.plain: The text traces a chain of essences, each the best part of the one before. The earth is the essence of all beings, and the chain runs through water, plants, people, speech and the sacred hymns. At the very top is Om.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-3.plain: Om is the best of all these essences. It is the highest and deserves the top place, as the eighth step in the chain.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-4.plain: The text asks a question. What really is the Rik (verse), the Saman (sung chant), and the udgitha (the chant of Om)?

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-5.plain: The text answers its question. The verse stands for speech, the chant stands for breath, and the udgitha is Om. Speech and breath belong together as a pair.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-6.plain: Speech and breath are joined together in the sound Om. When two partners come together, each gives the other what they wish for.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-7.plain: A person who understands this and meditates on Om will have their wishes fulfilled.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-8.plain: Om also means "yes." We say it whenever we agree to something, and saying yes brings satisfaction. A person who knows this and meditates on Om will satisfy wishes.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-9.plain: All the sacred rituals of the three Vedas, the oldest holy books, move forward through Om. Each priest says Om when he gives an order, recites, or sings, to honor the syllable. The ritual draws its power from Om.

upanishads-chandogya-1-1-10.plain: Someone might think that a person who understands Om and one who doesn't are doing the same ritual. But they are not, because knowing and not knowing are different. A ritual done with understanding and faith is more powerful.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-1.plain: A story begins. The Devas (gods) and the Asuras (demons), both children of Prajapati the creator, were fighting. The gods took up the chant of Om, hoping it would help them defeat the demons.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-2.plain: First the gods meditated on Om as the sense of smell in the nose. But the demons struck it with evil. That is why we smell both pleasant and bad smells.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-3.plain: Next the gods meditated on Om as speech, but the demons struck it with evil too. That is why people speak both truth and lies.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-4.plain: Then the gods meditated on Om as the eye, but the demons struck it with evil. That is why we see both beautiful and ugly things.
themes: what we choose to look at

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-5.plain: Then the gods meditated on Om as the ear, but the demons struck it with evil. That is why we hear both things we should hear and things we should not, like gossip.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-6.plain: Then the gods meditated on Om as the mind, but the demons struck it with evil. That is why we have both good thoughts and thoughts we should not have.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-7.plain: Next the gods meditated on Om as the breath of life that moves through the mouth. When the Asuras (demons) attacked it, they were smashed apart, like a lump of clay thrown against a hard rock.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-8.plain: A person who truly understands this becomes like a solid rock. Anyone who wishes him harm or attacks him will break apart, like clay hitting stone.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-9.plain: This breath in the mouth does not judge smells as good or bad, because it is free from evil. The food and drink it takes in keep all the senses alive. When a person is dying and can no longer find this breath, he leaves the body, and the mouth opens as if wanting to eat.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-10.plain: The sage Angiras meditated on Om as this breath. People call the breath Angiras because it is the essence (rasa) of the body's limbs (anga).

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-11.plain: The sage Brihaspati also meditated on Om as this breath. The breath is called Brihaspati because speech is called brihati, and breath is the lord (pati) of speech.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-12.plain: The sage Ayasya meditated on Om as this breath. The breath is called Ayasya because it comes (ayati) out of the mouth (asya).

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-13.plain: Vaka Dalbhya understood this teaching. He was the chief singer at a great sacrifice held in the Naimisha forest, and through his singing he won for the people what they wished for.

upanishads-chandogya-1-2-14.plain: Whoever knows this and meditates on Om as the breath of life in the mouth gets all his wishes by singing. This ends the teaching on Om in relation to the body.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-1.plain: Now comes meditation on Om in relation to the gods of nature. One should meditate on Om as the sun. When the sun rises, it sings for all living beings and takes away the fear of darkness. Whoever knows this can remove the fear of darkness, meaning ignorance.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-2.plain: The breath in the mouth and the sun are really the same. Both are warm. The breath is called sound and the sun is called echoing sound. So one should meditate on Om as both the breath and the sun.
themes: we are part of the universe

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-3.plain: One should also meditate on Om as vyana, the held breath. Breathing out is prana and breathing in is apana; the pause between them is vyana. Speech happens in that pause, because when we talk we neither breathe in nor out.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-4.plain: Speech becomes a verse of the Rig Veda, the verse becomes a sacred chant, and the chant becomes Om. So when a person recites a verse, sings a chant, or sings Om, he does it while holding the breath.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-5.plain: Other tasks that need strength, like making fire by rubbing sticks, running a race, or bending a strong bow, are also done while holding the breath. So one should meditate on Om as this held breath.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-6.plain: One should meditate on the three parts of the word udgitha. 'Ut' is breath, because breath makes a person rise. 'Gi' is speech, because words are called girah. 'Tha' is food, because food keeps everything standing.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-7.plain: The three parts of the word also stand for heaven, sky, and earth; for the sun, air, and fire; and for the three Vedas. Whoever meditates this way receives the gifts of speech and will have plenty of food and good health to enjoy it.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-8.plain: Next is how to have prayers fulfilled. Before singing, the priest should quickly think about the chant he is about to sing.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-9.plain: He should also quickly think of the verse the chant comes from, the sage who first saw or composed it, and the god he is going to praise.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-10.plain: He should think of the verse's rhythm and of the tune he will sing.

upanishads-chandogya-1-3-11.plain: He should think of the direction of the world he is praising, and finally of himself. Then, keeping his wish in mind and pronouncing every word correctly, he should sing. His wish will soon come true.

upanishads-chandogya-1-4-1.plain: One should meditate on the sacred syllable Om, because the chant always begins with Om. What follows is the full explanation of Om.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-3.plain: The starving Ushasti asks the chief for some of his leftover beans, and the chief gives them. When the chief also offers him water, Ushasti refuses, because drinking someone's leftover water would make him ritually unclean.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-4.plain: The chief asks why the leftover beans were acceptable if the water was not. Ushasti explains that he would have died without the beans, but there was other water to drink, so taking this water would only be for comfort.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-5.plain: After eating, Ushasti gives the rest of the beans to his wife. She had already found food, so she keeps them safe for later.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-6.plain: The next morning Ushasti wishes aloud for a little food so he would have the strength to earn some money. He knows the local king is holding a big sacrifice and hopes to be hired as its priest.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-7.plain: His wife hands him the beans she had saved. He eats them and goes to the king's sacrifice.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-8.plain: At the sacrifice, Ushasti sits near the priests who are about to sing the sacred hymns. He speaks to the Prastotri, the priest who sings the opening part.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-9.plain: Ushasti warns the Prastotri that if he sings his part without knowing which god it belongs to, his head will fall off.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-10.plain: Ushasti gives the same warning to the Udgatri, the priest who sings the main chant called the udgitha.

upanishads-chandogya-1-10-11.plain: He gives the same warning to the Pratihartri, the priest who sings the responding part. All three priests stop and sit in silence.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-1.plain: The king who is holding the sacrifice asks who this man is. He answers that he is Ushasti Kakrayana.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-2.plain: The king says he had searched for Ushasti to lead the sacrifice, but could not find him, so he hired other priests.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-3.plain: The king asks Ushasti to take charge of everything. Ushasti agrees but lets the other priests keep singing, asking only to be paid the same as them.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-4.plain: The Prastotri comes to Ushasti and humbly asks which god his part of the hymn belongs to.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-5.plain: Ushasti says the god is breath (prana), because all living beings come from breath and return into it. Singing without knowing this, after being warned, would have cost the priest his head.
themes: breath as the source of life

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-6.plain: The Udgatri also comes and asks which god his main chant belongs to.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-7.plain: Ushasti says it is the sun, because all beings praise the sun when it is high in the sky. Knowing this is needed to sing the chant properly.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-8.plain: The Pratihartri comes and asks which god his responding part belongs to.

upanishads-chandogya-1-11-9.plain: Ushasti says it is food (anna), because all beings live by eating food. Knowing this is needed to sing the hymn properly.

upanishads-chandogya-1-12-1.plain: A new story begins, called the chant of the dogs. A man named Vaka Dalbhya, also called Glava Maitreya, goes to a quiet place to recite the Veda, the sacred scripture.

upanishads-chandogya-1-12-2.plain: A white dog appears to him. Other dogs gather around the white dog and ask him to sing a chant to get them food, because they are hungry.

upanishads-katha-1-1-28.plain: Nachiketas asks Death a question. Who would want a long life full of beauty and love, once he has met the gods who never grow old? Every human body slowly wears out.

upanishads-katha-1-1-29.plain: Nachiketas will not take any other gift. He wants Death to explain what happens after we die, the question people argue about. He wants to know the hidden truth.

upanishads-katha-1-2-1.plain: Death (Yama) begins teaching. What is good for us and what feels pleasant are two different things, and both pull at us. Choosing the good goes well, but choosing only the pleasant makes a person miss life's true goal.
themes: doing the right thing vs the easy thing

upanishads-katha-1-2-2.plain: Both the good and the pleasant come to every person. A wise person looks at them carefully, tells them apart, and picks the good. A foolish person picks the pleasant because he is greedy.

upanishads-katha-1-2-3.plain: Death praises Nachiketas. He thought about every pleasure he was offered and turned them all down. He did not take the road of chasing wealth, where many people are ruined.

upanishads-katha-1-2-4.plain: Not knowing the truth and real wisdom are two very different roads that lead to different places. Death sees that Nachiketas truly wants wisdom, because all those pleasures could not pull him away.

upanishads-katha-1-2-5.plain: Some foolish people think they are clever and are proud of what they know. In fact they wander lost, like blind people being led by other blind people.

upanishads-katha-1-2-6.plain: A careless person dazzled by money never thinks about life after death. He thinks this world is all there is. Because of that, Death says, he falls into Death's power again and again.
themes: is this life all there is

upanishads-katha-1-2-7.plain: Many people never even hear about the Self, the true inner being in each of us. Many who hear about it still do not understand. A person who can teach it is rare and wonderful, and so is a person who understands it.

upanishads-katha-1-2-8.plain: If a poor teacher explains the Self, it is hard to grasp, even if you think about it a lot. You need a real teacher to show the way, because the Self is finer than the smallest thing.

upanishads-katha-1-2-9.plain: This truth cannot be reached by arguing. When a true teacher explains it, it becomes easy to understand. Death tells Nachiketas he has received it and praises his firm determination, wishing for more students like him.

upanishads-katha-1-2-10.plain: Nachiketas says he knows riches do not last, and things that pass away cannot buy what lasts forever. He performed the fire ritual named after him, and by using passing things that way he gained the lasting teaching of Yama.

upanishads-katha-1-2-11.plain: Yama says Nachiketas was shown every wish come true, great rewards, a place without fear, and lasting rest. Yet, being wise, he firmly put all of it aside.
themes: giving up rewards for something higher

upanishads-katha-1-2-12.plain: God, the ancient one, is hidden deep inside us, like something in a dark cave, and is hard to see. A wise person who finds God through meditation on the inner Self leaves both joy and sorrow far behind.

upanishads-katha-1-2-13.plain: A person who hears this teaching, takes it to heart, and sees the subtle inner Being apart from all outer qualities, feels true joy. Yama believes the door to Brahman, the highest reality, is open to Nachiketas.

upanishads-katha-1-2-14.plain: Nachiketas asks Yama to tell him about the reality that is beyond everything: beyond this and that, beyond cause and effect, beyond past and future.

upanishads-katha-1-2-15.plain: Yama answers briefly. The word all the holy books (the Vedas) speak of, which all spiritual effort aims at, and which students long for, is Om.

upanishads-katha-1-2-16.plain: The syllable Om never perishes, and it stands for Brahman, the highest reality. Whoever truly knows Om gains whatever he wishes for.

upanishads-katha-1-2-17.plain: Om is the best and highest support to lean on. Whoever knows this support is honored in the world of Brahma, the creator god.

upanishads-katha-1-2-18.plain: The Self, the knowing presence inside us, is never born and never dies. It has no beginning and lasts forever. When the body is killed, the Self is not killed.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-1.plain: Whoever understands what is oldest and best becomes the oldest and best himself. Breath is the oldest and best of all.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-2.plain: Whoever understands what is richest becomes the richest. Speech is the richest.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-3.plain: Whoever understands what gives firm footing stands firm in this life and the next. The eye gives firm footing, because seeing lets us stand steady.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-4.plain: Whoever understands success has his wishes come true, both spiritual and everyday ones. The ear is success, because hearing lets us learn.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-5.plain: Whoever understands the home becomes a home and support for his people. The mind is the home, where all our experiences gather.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-6.plain: The five senses (breath, speech, sight, hearing and mind) argued about which of them was the best. Each one said, "I am better."

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-7.plain: The senses went to their father Prajapati, the creator, and asked who was best. He told them that the best is the one whose leaving makes the body worst off.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-8.plain: Speech left the body for a year. When it came back, the others said they had lived like people who cannot talk, but still breathed, saw, heard and thought. So speech returned to its place.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-9.plain: Sight left for a year. The others lived like blind people, but still breathed, spoke, heard and thought. So the eye came back.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-10.plain: Hearing left for a year. The others lived like deaf people, but still breathed, spoke and thought. So the ear came back.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-11.plain: The mind left for a year. The others lived like small children whose minds are not yet grown, but still breathed, spoke, saw and heard. So the mind came back.
themes: even the mind is not everything

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-12.plain: When breath began to leave, it pulled all the other senses loose, like a horse ripping up its tether pegs. They begged breath to stay and called it their lord and the best of them.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-13.plain: Speech told breath that its own richness really belonged to breath. The eye said the same about its firm footing.

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-14.plain: The ear said its success really belonged to breath. The mind said its role as home really belonged to breath.
themes: recognizing the source of our gifts

upanishads-chandogya-5-1-15.plain: That is why people call all the senses "pranas," meaning breaths. All of them are really forms of breath, the life force.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-1.plain: Breath asked what its food would be. The senses said everything, even what dogs and birds eat. So breath is called Ana, the breather or eater, and for someone who knows this, no food is improper.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-2.plain: Breath asked what its clothing would be, and they said water. That is why wise people sip water before and after eating, so that breath is clothed and not naked.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-3.plain: The teacher Satyakama Jabala taught this to his student Goshruti. He said this teaching is so powerful that even a dry stick would sprout branches and leaves if told it.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-4.plain: Someone who wants greatness should begin a preparation rite at new moon. At full moon he mixes herbs with curd and honey, pours ghee (clarified butter) into the fire saying "Svaha to the oldest and best," and adds the leftover ghee to the mixture.

upanishads-chandogya-5-2-5.plain: He repeats the offering of ghee into the fire, saying "Svaha to the richest," then "to the firm rest," then "to success." Each time he adds the leftover ghee to the mixture.

upanishads-chandogya-4-8-1.plain: The swan tells Satyakama that a diver-bird will teach him the next part about Brahman, the ultimate reality behind everything. The next day Satyakama drives his teacher's cows on, and at evening he makes a fire, pens the cows, and sits facing east.

upanishads-chandogya-4-8-2.plain: A diver-bird flies near and calls Satyakama by name. He answers respectfully, 'Sir.'

upanishads-chandogya-4-8-3.plain: The diver-bird teaches that breath, eye, ear and mind together make up one part of Brahman, called 'having a home.' Whoever understands and meditates on this will have a home in this world and in the worlds beyond.
themes: the body and mind as sacred

upanishads-chandogya-4-9-1.plain: Satyakama finally reaches his teacher's house with the cows. The teacher calls his name and he answers, 'Sir.'
themes: a student meets his teacher again

upanishads-chandogya-4-9-2.plain: The teacher sees that Satyakama's face glows like someone who knows Brahman and asks who taught him. Satyakama says beings other than humans taught him, but he wants his teacher to be the one who teaches him.
themes: inner change shows on the face

upanishads-chandogya-4-9-3.plain: Satyakama explains he has heard that knowledge only truly helps when learned from a teacher. So the teacher taught him the same knowledge, leaving nothing out.

upanishads-chandogya-4-10-1.plain: A young man named Upakosala lived as a student in Satyakama's house and tended his sacred fires for twelve years. Satyakama let the other students finish and go home, but he would not let Upakosala leave.

upanishads-chandogya-4-10-2.plain: Satyakama's wife urges him to teach the worn-out student who has cared for his fires so well. But Satyakama leaves on a journey without teaching him.

upanishads-chandogya-4-10-3.plain: Upakosala is so sad he cannot eat. When the teacher's wife asks why, he says his many wishes pull him in different directions, and he is too full of sorrow to eat.

upanishads-chandogya-4-10-4.plain: The sacred fires that Upakosala had tended talk among themselves. They decide that because he cared for them so faithfully, they will teach him themselves.

upanishads-chandogya-4-10-5.plain: The fires teach that Brahman is breath, joy (Ka) and open space (Kha). Upakosala understands breath but not the other two, so they explain that joy and space are one, teaching him Brahman as breath and as the space in the heart.

upanishads-chandogya-4-11-1.plain: The household fire teaches that earth, fire, food and the sun are its forms. It says it is the same as the being seen in the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-4-11-2.plain: The fire says whoever knows this and meditates on it is freed from wrongdoing, lives a long full life, and his family line continues. The fires protect such a person in this world and the next.

upanishads-chandogya-4-12-1.plain: The southern fire teaches that water, the directions, the stars and the moon are its forms. It says it is the same as the being seen in the moon.

upanishads-chandogya-4-12-2.plain: Whoever knows this and meditates on it is freed from wrongdoing, lives long, and his family continues. The fires protect him in this world and the next.

upanishads-chandogya-4-13-1.plain: The eastern fire teaches that breath, space, sky and lightning are its forms. It says it is the same as the being seen in the lightning.

upanishads-chandogya-4-13-2.plain: Whoever knows this and meditates on it is freed from wrongdoing, lives long, and his family continues. The fires protect him in this world and the next.

upanishads-chandogya-4-14-1.plain: The fires together tell Upakosala they have given him their knowledge and the knowledge of the Self. But his teacher will show him the way forward.

upanishads-chandogya-4-14-2.plain: When Satyakama returns, he sees Upakosala's face glowing like one who knows Brahman and asks who taught him. Upakosala hints shyly that the fires did, and the teacher asks what they said.
themes: inner change shows on the face

upanishads-chandogya-4-14-3.plain: Upakosala repeats some of what the fires said. Satyakama says they only taught him about the worlds, and promises to teach something deeper: knowledge so pure that wrong deeds cannot stick to the one who knows it, like water rolls off a lotus leaf.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-8.plain: This is the chant the worshipper sings before the noon offering. He asks the gods to open the door of the sky so he can see them and live freely there.
themes: asking the gods for a place

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-9.plain: The worshipper makes his offering and bows to Vayu, the god of the air who lives in the sky. He asks Vayu to win that world for him.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-10.plain: The worshipper says he will go to the sky-world when this life ends. He hands over his offering, asks for the door to be unbolted, and stands up. The Rudras, a group of storm gods, then complete the noon offering for him.
themes: where we go when we die

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-11.plain: Before the third and final offering of the day, the worshipper sits behind the main fire altar, faces north, and sings a chant. It is for the Adityas (sun gods) and the Visve Devas (all the gods together).

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-12.plain: The chant to the Adityas, the sun gods, asks them to open the door of heaven. The worshipper wants to see them and rule over everything there.
themes: asking the gods for a place

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-13.plain: Next comes the same chant sung to the Visve Devas, all the gods together. Again he asks them to open heaven's door so he may see them and rule there.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-14.plain: The worshipper makes his offering and bows to the Adityas and the Visve Devas, who live in heaven. He asks them to win that heavenly world for him.

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-15.plain: The worshipper declares that heaven is his world and he will go there when this life ends. He gives his offering, asks for the door to be unbolted, and stands up.
themes: where we go when we die

upanishads-chandogya-2-24-16.plain: The Adityas and the Visve Devas complete the third offering for him. Whoever understands the meaning behind these steps understands the whole sacrifice.

upanishads-chandogya-3-1-1.plain: This begins a picture of the sun as honey enjoyed by the gods (Devas). Heaven is like a beam, the sky hangs from it like a beehive, and the shining mist is like the bees' eggs.
themes: the sun as a source of life
seeing the sacred in the sky

upanishads-chandogya-3-1-2.plain: The sun's eastern rays are like honeycomb cells. The verses of the Rig Veda, the oldest holy book, are the bees. The Rig Veda ritual is the flower, and the water poured in offering is its nectar.

upanishads-chandogya-3-1-3.plain: The Rig Veda verses worked over the ritual the way bees work over a flower. From it came fame, a glowing face, energy, strength and good health.

upanishads-chandogya-3-1-4.plain: This sweet essence flowed up to the sun. It is the red light we see when the sun rises.

upanishads-chandogya-3-2-1.plain: The sun's southern rays are like honeycomb cells on the right. The verses of the Yajur Veda, the book of ritual formulas, are the bees. Its ritual is the flower, and the offered water is the nectar.

upanishads-chandogya-3-2-2.plain: The Yajur Veda verses worked over the ritual like bees over a flower. From it came fame, a glowing face, energy, strength and good health.

upanishads-chandogya-3-2-3.plain: This sweet essence flowed up to the sun. It is the sun's white light.

upanishads-chandogya-3-3-1.plain: The sun's western rays are like honeycomb cells at the back. The verses of the Sama Veda, the book of sacred songs, are the bees. Its ritual is the flower, and the water is the nectar.

upanishads-chandogya-3-3-2.plain: The Sama Veda songs worked over the ritual like bees over a flower. From it came fame, a glowing face, energy, strength and good health.

upanishads-chandogya-3-3-3.plain: This sweet essence flowed up to the sun. It is the sun's dark light.

upanishads-chandogya-3-4-1.plain: The sun's northern rays are like honeycomb cells on the left. The hymns of the Atharva Veda are the bees. The old stories and legends (Itihasa-purana) are the flower, and the water is the nectar.

upanishads-chandogya-8-8-1.plain: Prajapati, the creator-teacher, tells his two students, Indra (king of the gods) and Virochana (king of the demons), to look at their reflections in a pan of water. They report that they see a complete copy of themselves, down to their hair and nails.

upanishads-chandogya-8-8-2.plain: Prajapati tells the two students to dress up in their best clothes, clean themselves, and look into the water again. Then he asks them what they see.
themes: is my appearance who I am

upanishads-chandogya-8-8-3.plain: The students say they see themselves dressed up and clean, just as they are. Prajapati says, "That is the Self, the deathless, the fearless, Brahman (the ultimate reality)," and both leave feeling satisfied.

upanishads-chandogya-8-8-4.plain: As they leave, Prajapati says that neither of them has truly understood the Self, and anyone who follows this idea will be ruined. Virochana goes home and teaches the demons that the body is the self, and that pampering and serving the body wins both this world and the next.

upanishads-chandogya-8-8-5.plain: That is why people still call someone who gives no charity, has no faith, and makes no offerings a demon-like person, because this is the demons' teaching. Such people decorate dead bodies with perfume, flowers and fine clothes, thinking this will win them the next world.

upanishads-chandogya-8-9-1.plain: On his way home, Indra sees a problem. If the reflection changes with the body, then it will be blind if the body is blind, lame if the body is lame, and it will die when the body dies. So he decides this teaching is no good.
themes: is the body all I am

upanishads-chandogya-8-9-2.plain: Indra goes back to Prajapati as a humble student carrying firewood, the custom for students. When asked why he returned, he explains his doubt: a self that follows the body will be hurt by its injuries and die with it.

upanishads-chandogya-8-9-3.plain: Prajapati agrees that Indra is right and promises to explain the true Self further. He asks Indra to stay and study with him for another thirty-two years, and Indra does.

upanishads-chandogya-8-10-1.plain: Prajapati now says the Self is the one who moves about happily in dreams. Indra leaves satisfied, but then thinks: it is true that the dreaming self is not blind or lame when the body is.
themes: who am I when I sleep

upanishads-chandogya-8-10-2.plain: Indra continues his doubt: even if the dream self is not hurt when the body is hurt, in dreams it still feels as if it is being beaten or chased. It feels pain and cries. So this answer is not good enough either.

upanishads-chandogya-8-10-3.plain: Indra returns to Prajapati again with firewood in his hands. He explains that the dream self is indeed free from the body's defects such as blindness or lameness.

upanishads-chandogya-8-10-4.plain: Indra says that in dreams the self still feels beaten and chased, feels pain and cries, so he sees no good in this answer. Prajapati agrees and asks him to stay another thirty-two years for further teaching, and Indra stays.

upanishads-chandogya-8-11-1.plain: Prajapati now says the Self is what remains in deep, dreamless sleep. Indra leaves satisfied but then worries: in deep sleep a person does not know "I am this," nor anything else, so it seems like being wiped out entirely.

upanishads-chandogya-8-11-2.plain: Indra goes back to Prajapati once more and explains his doubt: in deep sleep one knows neither oneself nor anything that exists, which seems like complete nothingness. He sees no good in that.

upanishads-chandogya-8-11-3.plain: Prajapati agrees and promises to explain the Self one last time. He asks Indra to stay five more years, making one hundred and one years of study in total.

upanishads-chandogya-8-12-1.plain: Prajapati teaches that the body is mortal and always in death's grip, but it is the home of the Self, which is deathless and has no body. As long as you think "I am this body," you are caught by pleasure and pain; when you know you are different from the body, pleasure and pain no longer touch you.

upanishads-chandogya-8-12-2.plain: Prajapati compares the Self to wind, clouds, lightning and thunder, which have no bodies. They rise from the sky and show their true form when they reach the highest light.

upanishads-chandogya-8-12-3.plain: In the same way, the peaceful Self rises from the body and shows its true form when it reaches the highest light, which is knowledge of the Self. Then it is the highest person, free and joyful, not caring about the body it was born in. The spirit is tied to the body like a horse to a cart.

upanishads-chandogya-8-12-4.plain: The eye, nose, tongue and ear are only tools for seeing, smelling, speaking and hearing. The Self is the one who knows and wants to see, smell, speak or hear.

upanishads-chandogya-8-12-5.plain: The Self is the one who thinks, and the mind is its divine eye, through which it sees and enjoys hidden joys. The gods meditate on this Self, so they have all worlds and desires, and anyone who knows and understands this Self gains the same.

upanishads-katha-2-2-2.plain: Death, teaching the boy Nachiketas, says that Brahman (the one ultimate reality) is present everywhere. It is the sun in the sky, the air, the fire on the hearth, and the holy drink in the ritual jar. It lives in people, in gods, in heaven, in water, on earth and on mountains. It is the True and the Great.

upanishads-katha-2-2-3.plain: Brahman is what makes us breathe in and breathe out. It sits at the center of the body, and all our senses serve it like worshippers.

upanishads-katha-2-2-4.plain: When the Self that lives in the body leaves it at death, what is left behind? Only the lifeless body. The Self was what truly mattered.

upanishads-katha-2-2-5.plain: We are not kept alive only by breathing in and out. We live because of something deeper, the Self, which the breath itself depends on.

upanishads-katha-2-2-6.plain: Death says to Nachiketas (here called Gautama, his family name) that he will now explain the ancient secret of Brahman and what happens to a person after death.

upanishads-katha-2-2-7.plain: After death, some beings are born again into a new body, and others become things like plants or stones. Where they go depends on what they did and what they understood in life.

upanishads-katha-2-2-8.plain: The highest Being stays awake inside us even while we sleep and creates our dreams. That is Brahman, the Immortal. All worlds rest in it, and nothing goes beyond it.
themes: what is awake when I sleep

upanishads-katha-2-2-9.plain: Fire is one thing, but it takes different shapes depending on what it burns. In the same way, the one Self lives in all things and looks different in each, yet it is also beyond them all.
themes: different on the outside, same inside

upanishads-katha-2-2-10.plain: Air is one, but it takes the shape of whatever it fills. In the same way, the one Self lives inside every being and seems different in each, yet it also stays beyond them.

upanishads-katha-2-2-11.plain: The sun lights up dirty things but does not become dirty. In the same way, the Self inside everyone is never stained by the world's suffering, because it stands apart from it.
themes: suffering can't touch my true self
staying pure in a hard world

upanishads-katha-2-2-12.plain: There is one ruler, the Self inside all things, who shows up in many forms. Those who find this Self inside themselves have lasting happiness; others do not.

upanishads-katha-2-2-13.plain: There is one eternal knower behind all our passing thoughts, and it answers the wishes of many beings. Those who find it inside themselves have lasting peace; others do not.

upanishads-katha-2-2-14.plain: The wise sense the highest joy, which words cannot describe, and simply say, "This is that." Nachiketas asks how he can understand it: does it shine by its own light, or does it reflect another light?

upanishads-katha-2-2-15.plain: Death answers that the sun, moon, stars, lightning and fire cannot light up Brahman. Instead, Brahman is the light that makes all these shine.

upanishads-katha-2-3-1.plain: The world is like an ancient tree that grows upside down: its roots are above in Brahman and its branches spread down into the world. That root is Brahman, the Immortal, which holds all worlds, and nothing goes beyond it.

upanishads-katha-2-3-2.plain: Everything in the world came out of Brahman and moves by its breath. Brahman is awesome and frightening, like a raised sword. Those who know it become immortal.

upanishads-katha-2-3-3.plain: Because of the awe of Brahman, fire burns and the sun shines. The gods Indra (king of the gods) and Vayu (the wind), and even Death itself, rush to do their jobs out of that same awe.

upanishads-katha-2-3-4.plain: If a person does not come to know Brahman before their body dies, they must be born again into another body.

upanishads-katha-2-3-5.plain: In this human life, Brahman can be seen clearly, like a face in a mirror. In other worlds it is seen less clearly: blurry like a dream in the world of the ancestors, shaky like a reflection in water in the world of heavenly singers, and only in the world of Brahma (the creator god) as clear as light is from shade.

upanishads-katha-2-3-6.plain: A wise person sees that the senses are separate from the true Self. Waking and sleeping belong to the senses, not to the Self. Knowing this, the wise person grieves no more.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-5.plain: The true Self is reached by being honest, by self-discipline, by right understanding, and by self-control. People who live pure, simple lives find it. It is pure, like a light shining inside the body.
themes: how to find my true self

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-6.plain: Truth wins in the end, not lies. Truth builds the road called "the way of the gods." On that road, the old sages, whose wants were satisfied, travel to the highest home of the True One.
themes: being honest when lying seems easier

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-7.plain: Brahman, the ultimate reality, shines great and divine, beyond what the mind can picture. It is smaller than the smallest thing. It is farther than the farthest place, yet it is right here. Those who truly see find it hidden in their own heart.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-8.plain: You cannot see the Self with your eyes, describe it in words, or grasp it with any sense. Hard practices and good deeds alone cannot reach it either. When your mind becomes clear and pure through knowledge, you see it as you meditate on it as one whole, without parts.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-9.plain: The subtle Self is known through the mind, here in the body where the breath works in five ways. People's thoughts are always tangled up with the senses. When the mind is made clear and pure, the Self shows itself.

upanishads-mundaka-3-1-10.plain: A person with a purified heart gets whatever state or goal he truly sets his mind on, for himself or for others. So anyone who wants happiness should honor a person who knows the Self.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-1.plain: The one who knows the Self knows Brahman's highest home, which holds everything and shines brightly. Wise people who honor that Person without chasing their own happiness move beyond the seed of rebirth.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-2.plain: A person who keeps making wishes and cravings in his mind is born again and again to chase them. But for someone who knows the true Self inside, all cravings fall away, even in this life.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-3.plain: You cannot reach the Self just by studying scripture, by being clever, or by learning a lot. The Self is reached by the one it chooses. To that person, the Self shows its own true nature.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-4.plain: Someone who is weak, careless, or does not meditate properly cannot reach the Self. But a wise person who works at it with strength, real effort, and right meditation enters the home of Brahman.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-5.plain: When sages reach the Self, they feel fully satisfied by that knowledge. Their strong desires are gone and they are at peace. Devoted to the Self, they become completely one with the One who is everywhere.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-6.plain: Those who live simply and set things aside understand clearly what Vedanta, the final teaching of the Vedas, points to. They purify themselves by giving things up. At death they become fully free in Brahma's worlds and enjoy the highest immortality.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-7.plain: At death, the parts of the wise person go back to the elements they came from. Their senses go back to the gods who rule them. Their actions and their Self become one with the highest, never-ending reality.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-8.plain: Rivers flow into the sea and lose their names and shapes. In the same way, a wise person lets go of name and form and joins the divine Person, who is greater than the greatest.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-9.plain: Whoever truly knows the highest Brahman becomes Brahman. No one in his family line will be ignorant of it. He moves beyond sorrow and wrongdoing. Free from the knots in his heart, he becomes immortal.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-10.plain: A verse from the Rig Veda says who should be taught this knowledge of Brahman. It is for those who have done their duties, know the Vedas, and are steady in faith. They should make offerings to the sacred fire, called Agni, with trust and carry out the vow of carrying fire on the head, as the Atharva tradition requires.

upanishads-mundaka-3-2-11.plain: Long ago the sage Angiras taught this truth. Someone who has not done the proper preparation should not study it. The Upanishad ends by bowing twice to the great sages.

upanishads-prashna-1-1.plain: Six seekers, all devoted to Brahman and searching for the highest truth, believed the respected sage Pippalada could teach them. So they carried firewood in their hands, the sign of humble students, and went to him.

upanishads-prashna-1-2.plain: The sage Pippalada told them to live with him one more year with self-discipline, self-control, and faith. After that they could ask anything. He promised to tell them all he knew.

upanishads-prashna-1-3.plain: Then Kabandhin Katyayana, one of the students, came to the sage and asked where all living creatures come from.

upanishads-chandogya-7-11-1.plain: The teacher Sanatkumara tells his student Narada that fire, meaning heat and light, is greater than water, because fire makes rain. People feel the heat or see lightning and say, "It will rain." So he says to meditate on fire.

upanishads-chandogya-7-11-2.plain: Whoever meditates on fire as Brahman (the highest reality) becomes bright and reaches bright worlds with no darkness. Narada asks if there is something greater than fire, and the teacher says yes.

upanishads-chandogya-7-12-1.plain: Space is greater than fire, because the sun, moon, stars and fire all exist in space. We call, hear and answer through space. We are happy when we are together in it and sad when apart. Everything is born in space and grows toward it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-12-2.plain: Whoever meditates on space as Brahman reaches wide, open worlds full of light, free from pressure and pain. Narada asks if there is something greater than space, and the teacher says yes.

upanishads-chandogya-7-13-1.plain: Memory is greater than space. Without memory, a crowd of people could not hear, notice or understand anything. It is through memory that we recognize our children and our animals. So meditate on memory.

upanishads-chandogya-7-13-2.plain: Whoever meditates on memory as Brahman has power as far as memory reaches. Narada asks if there is something greater than memory, and the teacher says yes.

upanishads-chandogya-7-14-1.plain: Hope is greater than memory. Hope is what moves memory to act. Because of hope, people study holy songs, do rituals, and wish for children, wealth, this world and the next. So meditate on hope.

upanishads-chandogya-7-14-2.plain: Whoever meditates on hope as Brahman has his wishes fulfilled, and his prayers are not wasted. Narada asks if there is something greater than hope, and the teacher says yes.

upanishads-chandogya-7-15-1.plain: Prana, the life-breath that keeps us alive, is greater than hope. Everything mentioned so far is held by life like spokes held by the center of a wheel. Father, mother, brother, sister, teacher and priest are all this life-breath.

upanishads-chandogya-7-15-2.plain: If someone speaks rudely to a father, mother, brother, sister, teacher or priest, people scold him and say, "Shame on you! You have insulted them."

upanishads-chandogya-7-15-3.plain: But after the life-breath has left their bodies, if someone pushes the bodies together with a poker and burns them on the funeral fire, no one says he is insulting them. This shows that the person was really the life in the body.
themes: what leaves us when we die

upanishads-chandogya-7-15-4.plain: Life-breath is everything. A person who sees and understands this becomes an ativadin, someone who can speak about the highest truth. If people call him that, he does not need to deny it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-16-1.plain: The teacher says the real ativadin is the one who speaks of the Highest as Truth itself. Narada says he wants that, and the teacher tells him he must first want to know the Truth. Narada says he does.

upanishads-chandogya-7-17-1.plain: Only a person who understands the Truth can speak the Truth. Without understanding, you cannot speak it. So we must want to understand. Narada says he wants to understand.

upanishads-chandogya-7-18-1.plain: Understanding comes from thinking things through. A person who does not reflect does not understand. So we must learn to reflect. Narada says he wants to learn this.

upanishads-chandogya-7-19-1.plain: A person reflects deeply only when they have faith. Without faith, a person does not reflect. So we must learn what faith is. Narada says he wants to learn it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-20-1.plain: Faith grows when a person stays close to and serves a spiritual teacher. Without this, a person does not have faith. So we must learn how to follow a teacher. Narada says he wants to learn it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-21-1.plain: A person truly follows a teacher only when they do their sacred duties. Without doing one's duties, a person does not truly follow the teacher. So we must learn about duty. Narada says he wants to learn it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-22-1.plain: A person does their duties only when they find joy within. Without that joy, a person does not act. So we must learn about this joy. Narada says he wants to learn it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-23-1.plain: The teacher says that true joy is the Infinite, called bhuman, meaning that which has no limits. There is no real joy in anything small or limited. Only the Infinite is joy. Narada says he wants to understand the Infinite.

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-1.plain: The heart is pictured as having five doorways, guarded by the senses. The eastern door is the in-breath, which is linked to the eye and the sun. Whoever meditates on it this way becomes bright-faced and healthy.

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-2.plain: The southern door of the heart is the breath that moves through the body, linked to the ear and the moon. Whoever meditates on it this way becomes happy and well known.

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-3.plain: The western door of the heart is the downward breath, linked to speech and to Agni, the god of fire. Whoever meditates on it this way gains a glowing face and good health.

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-4.plain: The northern door of the heart is the breath that digests and balances, linked to the mind and to Parjanya, the god of rain. Whoever meditates on it this way becomes well known and beautiful.

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-5.plain: The upper door of the heart is the rising breath, linked to the air and to open space. Whoever meditates on it this way becomes strong and great.

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-6.plain: These five breaths are servants of Brahman, the ultimate reality, and they guard the door to heaven. Whoever understands them will have a strong son in the family and will reach heaven himself.

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-7.plain: The light that shines above everything, in the highest world of all, is the very same light that is inside each person. The text promises to show proof of this.
themes: am I connected to something bigger

upanishads-chandogya-3-13-8.plain: The proof is the warmth you feel when you touch your body, and the humming sound you hear when you cover your ears. Meditate on these as Brahman, the ultimate reality, that you can feel and hear. Whoever does this becomes noticed and well known.
themes: proof that the divine is real

upanishads-chandogya-3-14-1.plain: Everything is Brahman, the ultimate reality: all things come from it, end in it and live by it. A person is shaped by what they deeply want and believe. What you set your heart on in this life decides what you become after death. So set your heart on the truth described next.
themes: what I focus on shapes me

upanishads-chandogya-3-14-2.plain: This describes the one to set your heart on. He is pure awareness and light, his thoughts are always true, and like open space he is everywhere but unseen. All actions, wishes, smells and tastes come from him. He holds everything, never needs to speak, and is never caught off guard.

upanishads-chandogya-3-14-3.plain: This Self lives inside my heart and is tinier than a grain of rice or a mustard seed. Yet this same Self is bigger than the earth, the sky, heaven and all the worlds together.

upanishads-chandogya-3-14-4.plain: The teacher Sandilya says that this Self inside my heart, the source of everything, is Brahman itself. When I die, I will go to it. A person who truly trusts this has no doubt left.

upanishads-chandogya-3-15-1.plain: The universe is pictured as a great chest that never wears out. The earth is its floor, the four directions are its sides, and the heavens are its lid. It is a treasure box holding all things.

upanishads-chandogya-3-15-2.plain: The four directions of this chest have special names, and the wind is called their child. Whoever knows the wind as the child of the directions will never have to weep for his sons. A father can pray: 'May I never mourn my sons.'

upanishads-chandogya-3-15-3.plain: This is a protective prayer for one's children. The parent says he turns for safety to the everlasting chest of the universe, to Prana (life-breath), and to the three worlds named Bhuh, Bhuvah and Svah, along with his children, naming each one.

upanishads-chandogya-3-15-4.plain: The prayer is explained: when I say I turn to Prana, the life-breath, I mean I turn to everything that exists.

upanishads-chandogya-3-15-5.plain: When I say I turn to Bhuh, I mean I turn to the earth, the sky and heaven.

upanishads-chandogya-3-15-6.plain: When I say I turn to Bhuvah, I mean I turn to fire, wind and the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-3-15-7.plain: When I say I turn to Svah, I mean I turn to the three sacred books, the Rig, Yajur and Sama Vedas. That is the full meaning of the prayer.

upanishads-chandogya-3-16-1.plain: A person's whole life is like a sacred offering made in three parts. The first twenty-four years are the morning offering, matching the twenty-four syllables of a sacred verse. These years belong to the Vasus, gods who are really our life-breaths, because they keep us alive.

upanishads-chandogya-6-11-2.plain: The father, Uddalaka, continues teaching his son. When life leaves one branch of a tree, that branch dries up, and when life leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dies. He tells his son to understand people in the same way.

upanishads-chandogya-6-11-3.plain: The body dries up and dies when the living Self leaves it, but the living Self itself never dies. This tiny hidden essence is the true self of everything, and the father tells Svetaketu, "You are that." The son asks to learn more, and the father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-12-1.plain: The father asks his son to bring a fruit of the banyan tree (Nyagrodha) and break it open. Inside are tiny seeds. When the son breaks a seed, he says he sees nothing at all.

upanishads-chandogya-6-12-2.plain: The father explains that the huge banyan tree grows out of that fine essence inside the seed, even though his son cannot see it.
themes: what we cannot see is real

upanishads-chandogya-6-12-3.plain: The father says, "Believe it, my son." That hidden essence is the real self of everything, the True, and Svetaketu is that too. The son asks to learn more, and the father agrees.
themes: faith in what you cannot see

upanishads-chandogya-6-13-1.plain: The father tells his son to put salt in water and come back in the morning. When asked to bring the salt back, the son cannot find it, because it has dissolved.

upanishads-chandogya-6-13-2.plain: The son tastes the water from the top, the middle and the bottom, and it is salty everywhere. The father explains that the True (Sat) is in the body in the same way: you cannot see it, but it is really there everywhere.

upanishads-chandogya-6-13-3.plain: The father repeats that this hidden essence is the real self of all things, the True, and that Svetaketu is that. The son asks to learn more, and the father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-14-1.plain: The father tells a story. A man is blindfolded, led away from his home in Gandhara (a region in the northwest), and left alone in a wild place. He turns in every direction and shouts that he was brought there blindfolded and abandoned.

upanishads-chandogya-6-14-2.plain: If someone removes the blindfold and points the way, the man can ask from village to village and finally get home. In the same way, a person who finds a teacher gains true knowledge. He only has to wait until this body ends, and then he is complete.

upanishads-chandogya-6-14-3.plain: The father again says that this hidden essence is the real self of everything, the True, and that Svetaketu is that. The son asks to learn more, and the father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-15-1.plain: When a man is dying, his family gathers and asks, "Do you know me?" He still recognizes them as long as his speech, mind, breath and body heat have not yet merged back into the Highest Being.
themes: family at the end of life

upanishads-chandogya-6-15-2.plain: Once his speech, mind, breath and heat merge back into the Highest Being, he no longer knows them. That same hidden essence is the real self of all, and Svetaketu is that. The son asks to learn more, and the father agrees.
themes: a loved one no longer recognizing you

upanishads-chandogya-6-16-1.plain: The father describes an old trial by ordeal. A man accused of theft denies it and must hold a red-hot axe. If he really stole and lies, he hides his true self behind a falsehood, and he is burned and killed.

upanishads-chandogya-6-16-2.plain: If the man did not steal, he is true to himself, holds the hot axe, is not burned, and is set free. Just as truth protects that man, everything has its true self in the True, and Svetaketu is that. This time the son truly understood.

upanishads-chandogya-7-1-1.plain: Narada, a famous sage, comes to the teacher Sanatkumara and asks to be taught. Sanatkumara asks him first to say what he already knows, so he can teach him what lies beyond it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-1-2.plain: Narada lists everything he has studied: the four Vedas (sacred books), history and legends, grammar, rituals for ancestors, math, logic, ethics, astronomy, weapons, the arts and many other subjects. He says he knows all of it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-1-3.plain: Narada admits that with all his learning he only knows words and books, not the Self. He has heard that knowing the Self ends sorrow, and he is full of sorrow, so he asks for help. Sanatkumara says that everything he has read is only a name.

upanishads-chandogya-7-1-4.plain: Sanatkumara says that all of Narada's subjects, from the Vedas to the arts, are only names. He tells Narada to meditate on the name as a first step.

upanishads-chandogya-7-1-5.plain: Sanatkumara says that whoever meditates on the name as Brahman (the ultimate reality) has power only as far as names reach. Narada asks if there is something greater than a name, and the teacher says yes.

upanishads-chandogya-2-10-6.plain: A person who understands this and meditates on the seven-part chant (the Sâman, a sacred sung hymn) as one whole wins victory over death, pictured here as the sun. He also gains something even higher, a victory that carries him beyond death.
themes: seeing the whole, not just parts

upanishads-chandogya-2-11-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to parts of a person. The opening sound (hinkâra) is the mind, the introduction is speech, the main chant (udgîtha) is sight, the response is hearing, and the ending is breath. This is the Gâyatra chant found in our life-breaths (prânas).

upanishads-chandogya-2-11-2.plain: Whoever understands the Gâyatra chant this way keeps all their senses, lives a long, full life, and is blessed with family, wealth and a good name. The rule for such a person is: do not be proud.

upanishads-chandogya-2-12-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to the life of a fire. Rubbing the fire-stick is the opening, rising smoke is the introduction, burning flame is the main chant, glowing coals are the response, and the fire dying down and going out is the ending. This is the Rathantara chant found in fire.

upanishads-chandogya-2-12-2.plain: Whoever understands the Rathantara chant in fire becomes bright and strong, lives long, and is blessed with family, wealth and fame. The rule is: do not rinse your mouth or spit in front of a fire.

upanishads-chandogya-2-13-1.plain: Next the text turns to the Vâmadevya chant, which is linked to the creation of new life.

upanishads-chandogya-2-14-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to the sun's journey across the day: rising, fully risen, noon, afternoon, and setting. This is the Brihat chant found in the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-2-14-2.plain: Whoever understands the Brihat chant in the sun becomes shining and strong, lives long, and is blessed with family, wealth and fame. The rule is: never complain about the heat of the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-2-15-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to a rainstorm: mist gathering, the cloud rising, the rain falling, the lightning and thunder, and the rain stopping. This is the Vairûpa chant found in Parganya, the god of rain.

upanishads-chandogya-2-15-2.plain: Whoever understands the Vairûpa chant in the rain gains many kinds of animals, lives long, and is blessed with family, wealth and fame. The rule is: never complain about the rain.

upanishads-chandogya-2-16-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to the seasons: spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn and winter. This is the Vairâga chant found in the seasons.

upanishads-chandogya-2-16-2.plain: Whoever understands the Vairâga chant in the seasons shines through their children, animals and a glowing face, lives long, and gains wealth and fame. The rule is: never complain about the seasons.

upanishads-chandogya-2-17-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to the world: the earth, the sky, heaven, the directions, and the sea. These are the Sakvari chants found in the worlds.

upanishads-chandogya-2-17-2.plain: Whoever understands the Sakvari chants in the worlds comes to own the worlds, lives long, and is blessed with family, wealth and fame. The rule is: never complain about the world.
themes: accepting the world as it is

upanishads-chandogya-2-18-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to living beings: goats, sheep, cows, horses and humans. These are the Revati chants found in animals.

upanishads-chandogya-2-18-2.plain: Whoever understands the Revati chants in animals becomes rich in animals, lives long, and gains family, wealth and fame. The rule is: never complain about animals.

upanishads-chandogya-2-19-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to the body: hair, skin, flesh, bone and marrow. This is the Yagñâyagñîya chant found in the parts of the body.

upanishads-chandogya-2-19-2.plain: Whoever understands this chant in the body gets strong, whole limbs, lives long, and gains family, wealth and fame. The rule is: do not eat marrow for a year, or do not eat it at all.

upanishads-chandogya-2-20-1.plain: The five parts of the chant are matched to the gods of nature: fire, air, the sun, the stars and the moon. This is the Râgana chant found in the gods.

upanishads-chandogya-2-20-2.plain: Whoever understands the Râgana chant in the gods reaches the same world, happiness and company as the gods, and lives a long life with family, wealth and fame. The rule is: do not speak badly of the Brâhmanas, the priests and teachers.

upanishads-chandogya-7-24-1.plain: The teacher Sanatkumara tells his student Narada that the Infinite is the state where you no longer see, hear or know anything separate from yourself. Wherever there is a 'me' and a separate 'other', that is the limited world, and it dies. The Infinite does not die, and it rests on nothing but itself.

upanishads-chandogya-7-24-2.plain: Sanatkumara explains that he does not mean greatness the way people usually mean it. Cattle, gold, servants, family, land and houses are called greatness, but then the owner depends on something outside himself. The Infinite depends on nothing else.
themes: wealth does not make you whole

upanishads-chandogya-7-25-1.plain: The Infinite is everywhere: below, above, behind, in front, to the right and to the left. It is all of this. Then the teacher says the same thing using 'I': I am below, above and on every side. I am all this.

upanishads-chandogya-7-25-2.plain: The teacher says it again using 'the Self', meaning your deepest true being: the Self is on every side and is all this. A person who truly understands this loves and delights in the Self. That person rules himself and is free everywhere. Those who think otherwise stay under the control of others and live in a world that passes away.

upanishads-chandogya-7-26-1.plain: For someone who understands this, everything comes from the Self: breath and life, hope, memory, space, fire, water, birth and death, food, strength, thinking, will, mind, speech, names, holy hymns and rituals. All of it springs from the Self.

upanishads-chandogya-7-26-2.plain: An old verse says that whoever sees this truth does not see death, sickness or pain, and gains everything. The One becomes the many things of the world. When what we take in through our senses and mind is pure, our whole nature becomes pure, our memory of the true Self stays steady, and everything that binds us comes loose. In this way the wise Sanatkumara, also called Skanda, washed away Narada's faults and led him beyond darkness.
themes: being careful what you take in

upanishads-chandogya-8-1-1.plain: The body is like a city where God, called Brahman, lives. Inside it is a small palace shaped like a lotus flower, which is the heart. Inside the heart is a small open space. What lives in that space is what we should look for and come to understand.

upanishads-chandogya-8-1-2.plain: The teacher imagines students asking a question: in this body-city, with the heart and the tiny space inside it, what could be there that is worth looking for and understanding?

upanishads-chandogya-8-1-3.plain: The answer is that the space inside the heart is as big as all of space outside. Heaven and earth, fire and air, sun and moon, lightning and stars, and everything that is, was or will be are all held within it.

upanishads-chandogya-8-1-4.plain: Then students might ask: if everything is held inside the body, what is left when old age wears the body down or it falls apart in death?

upanishads-chandogya-8-1-5.plain: The answer is that what lives in the heart does not grow old when the body grows old, and it is not killed when the body dies. That is the real city of Brahman, not the body. It is the true Self, free from wrongdoing, old age, death, sadness, hunger and thirst, and it wants only what is truly right. The teacher begins to compare this with people on earth, who obey orders and depend on whatever land or thing they are attached to.

upanishads-chandogya-8-1-6.plain: Everything gained by hard work on earth eventually disappears. In the same way, rewards in the next life earned through rituals and good deeds also run out. People who die without finding the true Self and its true desires are not free anywhere. Those who find them are free in all worlds.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-1.plain: A person who has found the true Self only has to wish to meet his ancestors, the 'fathers', and they come to welcome him. He is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-2.plain: If such a person wishes to be with the world of mothers, the mothers come to welcome him just by his wish, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-3.plain: If such a person wishes to be with his brothers, they come to welcome him just by his wish, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-4.plain: If such a person wishes to be with his sisters, they come to welcome him just by his wish, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-5.plain: If such a person wishes to be with his friends, they come to welcome him just by his wish, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-6.plain: If such a person wishes for perfumes and flower garlands, they come to him just by his wish, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-7.plain: If such a person wishes for food and drink, they come to him just by his wish, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-8-2-8.plain: If such a person wishes for song and music, they come to him just by his wish, and he is happy.

upanishads-chandogya-1-4-2.plain: The Devas (the gods) were afraid of death, so they turned to the rituals of the three Vedas, the oldest sacred books. They wrapped themselves in the holy verses for protection, and that is why the verses are called khandas, meaning "coverings."

upanishads-chandogya-1-4-3.plain: Death still saw the gods inside their rituals, the way a fisherman spots a fish in clear water. When the gods noticed this, they left the rituals behind and went into Om, the sacred sound, by meditating on it.

upanishads-chandogya-1-4-4.plain: When a student finishes learning any of the Vedas, he says Om out loud. Om never decays, cannot die, and has no fear in it, and because the gods entered it, they became immortal and fearless.

upanishads-chandogya-1-4-5.plain: Anyone who understands this and chants Om enters that same deathless, fearless sound. Having entered it, that person becomes immortal, just like the gods.

upanishads-chandogya-1-5-1.plain: The udgitha, the main chanted hymn, and the pranava, the sound Om, are the same thing. Both are like the sun, because the sun moves across the sky as if sounding Om.
