upanishads-chandogya-1-5-2.plain: The sage Kaushitaki told his son that he had worshipped only the sun itself, and that is why he had only one son. He told his son to meditate on the sun's many rays as well, so he would be blessed with many sons.
themes: seeing the many in the one

upanishads-chandogya-1-5-3.plain: Turning to the human body, a person should meditate on the chanted hymn as the breath, because breath moves as if sounding Om.

upanishads-chandogya-1-5-4.plain: Kaushitaki told his son that he had worshipped breath as only one thing, and so he had only one son. He told his son to honor breath in its many forms if he wanted many sons.

upanishads-chandogya-1-5-5.plain: Whoever knows that the chanted hymn and Om are the same can fix any mistake the singing priest makes during the ritual. He can do this even from his own seat as the reciting priest.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-1.plain: The Rig Veda's verses are like the earth and the Sama Veda's songs are like fire, and fire rests on the earth. In the same way, the song rests on the verse. The word Sama is split into Sa, the earth, and ama, fire.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-2.plain: Here the verse is compared to the sky and the song to the air, because the air rests in the sky. That is why the song is sung resting on the verse.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-3.plain: The verse is compared to heaven and the song to the sun, which shines in heaven. So the song rests on the verse, as the sun rests in the heavens.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-4.plain: The verse is compared to the stars and the song to the moon, which moves among the stars. So the song rests on the verse.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-5.plain: The verse is compared to the sun's bright white light, and the song to the deep dark blue inside the sun. The darkness rests on the brightness, just as the song rests on the verse.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-6.plain: Sa is the sun's white light and ama is its dark blue, and together they make Sama. Then the text begins describing a golden person seen inside the sun, golden from his beard and hair down to his fingernails.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-7.plain: This golden person in the sun has eyes like blue lotus flowers. His name is Ut, meaning "risen," because he has risen above all evil, and whoever knows this also rises above all evil.

upanishads-chandogya-1-6-8.plain: The verse and the song are like the golden person's joints, so he is the sacred chant itself, and the priest who sings it is named after him. He rules the worlds above the sun and grants the wishes of the gods who live there.

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-1.plain: Now about the human body: the verse is like speech and the song is like breath, since breath rests on speech. Sa is speech and ama is breath, and together they make Sama.

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-2.plain: The verse is like the eye and the song is like the self, the image seen in the eye. So the song rests on the verse, as the reflection rests in the eye.

upanishads-chandogya-1-7-3.plain: The verse is like the ear and the song is like the mind, because the mind depends on what the ear hears. Sa is the ear and ama is the mind, and together they make Sama.

upanishads-chandogya-5-8-2.plain: The teacher continues: in the woman, seen as a sacred fire, the life-forces offer seed, and from this offering a child begins to form.

upanishads-chandogya-5-9-1.plain: This is why water, after passing through five sacred "offerings," becomes a human being. The tiny child grows hidden in the womb for about ten months and is then born.

upanishads-chandogya-5-9-2.plain: Once born, a person lives for however long their life lasts. When they die, friends carry them to the funeral fire, the same fire they first came from.

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-1.plain: People who understand this teaching, whether family people at home or seekers living in the forest with faith and self-discipline, travel after death along a path of brightness: light, day, the bright half of the month, the sun's northern journey, the year, the sun, the moon, and lightning. There they meet a being who is not human.
themes: spiritual seekers at home or in retreat

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-2.plain: That non-human being leads them to Brahman, the highest reality in a form that can be reached. This is called the path of the gods (Devas).

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-3.plain: But people who live in the village doing rituals, public good works, and giving charity go another way after death: through smoke, night, the dark half of the month, and the sun's southern months. They do not reach the year.

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-4.plain: From there they go to the world of the ancestors, then to the sky, then to the moon, which is Soma, the king. There the gods enjoy them as their food.

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-5.plain: They stay on the moon until the reward of their good deeds runs out. Then they come back the same way, through sky and air, becoming smoke and then mist.
themes: the cycle of life and death

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-6.plain: The mist becomes a cloud and falls as rain, and they are born as rice, grain, plants, trees, sesame, and beans. Getting out of this stage is very hard, because they become part of whoever eats that food and has children.
themes: the cycle of life and death
how life is connected to food

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-7.plain: Those who behaved well are soon born into a good life, such as a priestly, warrior, or merchant family. Those who behaved badly are soon born into a low life, such as a dog, a pig, or an outcaste.

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-8.plain: Tiny creatures like flies and worms follow neither path; they just keep being born and dying over and over in a third place. That is why the other world never fills up. So, the teacher says, a person should take care of their own soul.

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-9.plain: A verse says that four kinds of people fall: one who steals gold, one who drinks alcohol, one who sleeps with his teacher's wife, and one who kills a priest. A fifth is the person who keeps company with them.

upanishads-chandogya-5-10-10.plain: But a person who truly understands this teaching of the five fires is not stained by sin, even if they mix with such people. They stay pure and reach the world of the blessed.

upanishads-chandogya-5-11-1.plain: Five respected family men and great thinkers met and talked about a big question: What is our true Self, and what is Brahman, the ultimate reality?

upanishads-chandogya-5-11-2.plain: After thinking it over, they decided to visit Uddalaka Aruni, who was known to understand the universal Self called Vaisvanara. So they went to him.

upanishads-chandogya-5-11-3.plain: Uddalaka worried that these great scholars would question him and he would not be able to answer everything, so he decided to send them to another teacher.

upanishads-chandogya-5-11-4.plain: Uddalaka told them that King Asvapati Kaikeya understood the Vaisvanara Self, and suggested they all go to him together. They went.

upanishads-chandogya-5-11-5.plain: When they arrived, King Asvapati gave each of them gifts. The next morning he told them his kingdom had no thieves, misers, drunkards, ignorant people, or adulterers, and every home kept a sacred fire. He invited them to stay for his sacrifice and promised them rich payment.

upanishads-chandogya-5-11-6.plain: The men replied that a visitor should say why he has come. They told the king they came not for wealth but to learn about the Vaisvanara Self.
themes: being honest about why you came

upanishads-chandogya-5-11-7.plain: The king said he would answer the next day. In the morning they came to him humbly, carrying firewood like students, and he began teaching them without asking for the usual formal ceremonies.

upanishads-chandogya-2-6-1.plain: The Sâman is a sacred chant sung in five parts. Here the teacher says to think of those five parts as five kinds of animals: goats, sheep, cows, horses, and finally human beings.

upanishads-chandogya-2-6-2.plain: A person who understands this and meditates on the chant as animals will have many animals. In old times, owning animals meant being wealthy.

upanishads-chandogya-2-7-1.plain: The five parts of the sacred chant can also be seen as the senses and powers in us: smell, speech, sight, hearing, and mind. The text calls these prânas, meaning life-powers. Each one is greater than the one before it, and the mind is the greatest.

upanishads-chandogya-2-7-2.plain: A person who meditates on the chant as the senses gains what is greatest. He wins worlds that are greater than great.

upanishads-chandogya-2-8-1.plain: Now the teacher describes a chant with seven parts, found in speech itself. Certain sounds in words stand for the parts of the chant. 'Hun' is the first part, 'pra' the second, and 'â' is the 'first' part, which is linked to Om, the most sacred sound.

upanishads-chandogya-2-8-2.plain: The list goes on. 'Ud' is the main sung part, 'pra' is the response, 'upa' is the closing-in part, and 'ni' is the ending.

upanishads-chandogya-2-8-3.plain: For someone who meditates on the seven-part chant in speech, speech gives its best gifts, like a cow giving milk. That person has plenty of food and a healthy appetite to enjoy it.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-1.plain: One can also meditate on the seven-part chant as the sun. The sun is called Sâman because it is always the same (sama). Everyone feels the sun is looking right at them.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-2.plain: All living beings depend on the sun. The time before sunrise is the first part of the chant, and animals belong to it. That is why animals make the sound 'hin' before dawn.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-3.plain: The sun just after it rises is the second part of the chant, called the prastâva, and humans belong to it. That is why people love praise and fame.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-4.plain: The sun in mid-morning is the 'first' part, linked to Om, and birds belong to it. That is why birds can fly in the sky with nothing holding them up.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-5.plain: The sun at noon is the main sung part of the chant, and the Devas, the shining gods, belong to it. That is why they are the best of all the children of Pragâpati, the creator.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-6.plain: The sun in early afternoon is the response part of the chant. Unborn babies and seeds in the womb depend on it. That is why, once conceived, they hold on and do not fall away.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-7.plain: The sun in late afternoon is the closing-in part of the chant, and wild animals belong to it. That is why they run to the forest to hide when they see a person.

upanishads-chandogya-2-9-8.plain: The setting sun is the ending part of the chant, and the ancestors who have died belong to it. That is why people lay down offerings for them. This is how to meditate on the seven-part chant as the sun.

upanishads-chandogya-2-10-1.plain: Now the teacher describes a seven-part chant that is balanced and carries a person beyond death. He counts the syllables in the names of its parts. The first two names each have three syllables, so they are equal.

upanishads-chandogya-2-10-2.plain: The next name has two syllables and the one after has four. If you move one syllable from the longer to the shorter, they become equal.

upanishads-chandogya-2-10-3.plain: The name of the main sung part has three syllables and the next name has four. The extra syllable is set aside, so both count as three and are equal.

upanishads-chandogya-2-10-4.plain: The name of the ending part has three syllables, so it is balanced too. All the names together have twenty-two syllables.

upanishads-chandogya-2-10-5.plain: With twenty-one syllables a person reaches the sun, which is the twenty-first world from here and also stands for death. With the twenty-second syllable he goes beyond the sun, to a place of happiness with no sorrow.

upanishads-chandogya-6-3-2.plain: The father, Uddalaka, tells his son Svetaketu that the one Being, after making fire, water and earth, decided to enter into them as the living Self. Then it would give everything its names and shapes.

upanishads-chandogya-6-3-3.plain: The Being mixed fire, water and earth so each one also holds a little of the other two. Then it entered them as the living Self and gave things their names and forms.

upanishads-chandogya-6-3-4.plain: The father says the Being mixed all three elements together. He tells his son he will now explain how this mixing works.

upanishads-chandogya-6-4-1.plain: The father says a burning fire has red, white and black colors, which come from fire, water and earth. The word "fire" is only a name we speak. What is really there are those three basic parts.

upanishads-chandogya-6-4-2.plain: The sun is also made of the red of fire, the white of water and the black of earth. "Sun" is just a name. The three basic parts are what is real.

upanishads-chandogya-6-4-3.plain: The moon too is made of the red of fire, the white of water and the black of earth. "Moon" is just a name. The three basic parts are what is real.

upanishads-chandogya-6-4-4.plain: Lightning too is made of the red of fire, the white of water and the black of earth. "Lightning" is just a name. The three basic parts are what is real.

upanishads-chandogya-6-4-5.plain: Wise people of long ago, both family heads and religious scholars, knew this. They said nobody could tell them anything new, because by knowing these three basic parts they understood everything.

upanishads-chandogya-6-4-6.plain: These wise people saw anything red as coming from fire, anything white as coming from water, and anything black as coming from earth.
themes: seeing the simple behind the complex

upanishads-chandogya-6-4-7.plain: Even things that seemed strange and unknown, the wise knew were some mix of the three basic parts. Then the father says he will explain how these three parts work inside a person.
themes: seeing the simple behind the complex

upanishads-chandogya-6-5-1.plain: The father explains that food we eat splits three ways. The roughest part becomes waste, the middle part becomes flesh, and the finest part becomes the mind.

upanishads-chandogya-6-5-2.plain: Water we drink also splits three ways. The roughest part becomes urine, the middle part becomes blood, and the finest part becomes breath.

upanishads-chandogya-6-5-3.plain: Rich foods like oil and butter, which carry fire, split three ways. The roughest part becomes bone, the middle part becomes marrow, and the finest part becomes speech.

upanishads-chandogya-6-5-4.plain: The father sums up: the mind comes from food, breath from water, and speech from fire. His son Svetaketu asks to learn more, and the father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-6-1.plain: The father gives an example. When you churn yogurt, its finest part rises to the top and becomes butter.

upanishads-chandogya-6-6-2.plain: In the same way, the finest part of the food we eat rises up and becomes the mind.
themes: what we eat affects our thinking

upanishads-chandogya-6-6-3.plain: The finest part of the water we drink rises up and becomes breath.

upanishads-chandogya-6-6-4.plain: The finest part of rich, fiery food rises up and becomes speech.

upanishads-chandogya-6-6-5.plain: The father repeats that mind comes from food, breath from water, and speech from fire. His son asks to learn more, and the father agrees.

upanishads-chandogya-6-7-1.plain: The father says a person is made of sixteen parts. He tells his son to eat no food for fifteen days but drink as much water as he wants, since water keeps the breath alive.

upanishads-chandogya-1-12-3.plain: The white dog told the hungry dogs to come back to him the next morning. The sage Vaka Dalbhya, also called Glava Maitreya, stayed to watch what would happen.

upanishads-chandogya-1-12-4.plain: The dogs arrived in a line, each holding the tail of the dog in front in its mouth. This is how priests walk when they go to sing a sacred hymn. Then they sat down and began chanting the sound "Hin."

upanishads-chandogya-1-12-5.plain: The dogs chanted a prayer only for their own food and drink. They called on the gods Varuna, Prajapati and Savitri, saying "Om, let us eat! Om, let us drink! Lord of food, bring us food!"
themes: depending on a higher power for food

upanishads-chandogya-1-13-1.plain: The extra sounds sung in sacred chants each stand for something. Hau stands for the earth, Hai for the air, Atha for the moon, Iha for the self, and I for fire.

upanishads-chandogya-1-13-2.plain: More chant sounds are matched with things. U is the sun, E is calling out to the gods, Auhoi is all the gods together, and Hin is Prajapati, the creator. The tone is breath, Ya is food, and Vag is Viraj, the cosmic whole.

upanishads-chandogya-1-13-3.plain: The thirteenth chant sound, the unclear sound "Hun," stands for what cannot be described: Brahman, the highest reality.

upanishads-chandogya-1-13-4.plain: Whoever knows this secret teaching about the chants gets the full reward of speech, like milk from a cow. That person has plenty of food and the health to enjoy it.

upanishads-chandogya-2-1-1.plain: It is good to meditate on the whole Saman, the sacred chant. People even use the word "Saman" to mean "good," and say something bad is "not Saman."

upanishads-chandogya-2-1-2.plain: People also say someone came "with Saman" when they behaved properly. They say someone came "without Saman" when they behaved rudely.

upanishads-chandogya-2-1-3.plain: When something helps us, people say "this is Saman for us." When it does not help, they say "this is not Saman for us."

upanishads-chandogya-2-1-4.plain: Someone who understands this and meditates on the chant as goodness itself will quickly gain good qualities. Those qualities will become truly their own.
themes: power of what we dwell on

upanishads-chandogya-2-2-1.plain: A person should meditate on the five parts of the sacred chant as five worlds, going upward. The parts match the earth, fire, the sky, the sun and heaven.

upanishads-chandogya-2-2-2.plain: The same five parts can also be matched going downward: heaven, the sun, the sky, fire and the earth.

upanishads-chandogya-2-2-3.plain: Whoever understands this and meditates on the five-part chant as the worlds wins all the worlds, both upward and downward.
themes: feeling at home in the universe

upanishads-chandogya-2-3-1.plain: A person should meditate on the five-part chant as a rainstorm. The first part is the wind before rain, then the cloud arriving, then the rain falling, then the lightning and thunder.

upanishads-chandogya-2-3-2.plain: The last part is the rain stopping. Whoever meditates on the chant this way gets rain when they need it and can bring rain to others.

upanishads-chandogya-2-4-1.plain: A person should meditate on the five-part chant in all waters. The parts are clouds gathering, rain falling, rivers flowing east, rivers flowing west, and finally the sea.

upanishads-chandogya-2-4-2.plain: Whoever meditates on the chant as all waters will not drown and will always have plenty of water.

upanishads-chandogya-2-5-1.plain: A person should meditate on the five-part chant as the seasons. The parts are spring, summer harvest, the rainy season, autumn and winter.

upanishads-chandogya-2-5-2.plain: Whoever meditates on the chant as the seasons will be in step with every season. Things will go well for them at the right time.

upanishads-katha-1-3-14.plain: Wake up and get moving! You have been given great gifts, so learn to understand them. The wise say the path to finding your true Self is as hard to walk as the sharp edge of a razor.

upanishads-katha-1-3-15.plain: The true Self cannot be heard, touched, seen, tasted or smelled. It never ages, never began and never ends. A person who comes to know it is set free from the grip of death.

upanishads-katha-1-3-16.plain: A wise person who tells or hears this old story of Nachiketas, the boy who was taught by Death, is honored in the world of Brahman, the highest reality.

upanishads-katha-1-3-17.plain: Whoever recites this deep teaching to a gathering of priests, or with devotion during the Shraddha, the ceremony honoring dead ancestors, gains endless rewards.

upanishads-katha-2-1-1.plain: Death, still teaching the boy Nachiketas, says the Creator made our senses point outward, so people look out at the world instead of inward. But a wise person who wanted to live forever closed his eyes, looked within, and saw the true Self.

upanishads-katha-2-1-2.plain: Foolish people chase outside pleasures and get caught in the trap of death. Wise people know what lasts forever, so they do not look for anything lasting in this changing world.
themes: emptiness after getting what you want

upanishads-katha-2-1-3.plain: The same inner Self that lets us see, taste, smell, hear and feel touch is what knows everything else too. Death tells Nachiketas this is the answer he asked for.

upanishads-katha-2-1-4.plain: The one who sees and knows things, whether we are awake or dreaming, is the great Self that is everywhere. A wise person who understands this stops grieving.

upanishads-katha-2-1-5.plain: The living soul that enjoys life's experiences is the true Self. It is always close by and rules over past and future. Whoever knows this is no longer afraid.

upanishads-katha-2-1-6.plain: The Self is the first being that came out of the creative heat, even before water existed. It lives in the heart and shows itself through the world's elements. This is the Self Death is describing.

upanishads-katha-2-1-7.plain: The Self is also Aditi, the mother of the gods, who holds all the gods within her. She comes forth with the breath of life, lives in the heart and appears through the elements. This too is that Self.

upanishads-katha-2-1-8.plain: Agni, the fire god who sees everything, hides in the two sticks rubbed together to make fire, guarded like a baby in its mother's womb. People worship it every morning with offerings. This fire is also that Self.

upanishads-katha-2-1-9.plain: The place the sun rises from and sets into holds all the gods, and nothing goes beyond it. That is the Self.

upanishads-katha-2-1-10.plain: What we see in this world is the same as Brahman, the unseen highest reality, and Brahman is the same as this world. Whoever thinks they are separate keeps going from one death to another.

upanishads-katha-2-1-11.plain: Brahman can be reached through a focused mind, and then you see no difference at all between things. Whoever keeps seeing separation goes from death to death.

upanishads-katha-2-1-12.plain: The inner Person, said to be the size of a thumb, lives in the middle of the body. It rules past and future. Whoever knows it no longer fears.

upanishads-katha-2-1-13.plain: This thumb-sized inner Person is like a clean flame with no smoke. It rules past and future, and it stays the same today and tomorrow.

upanishads-katha-2-1-14.plain: Rain falling on a mountain top runs off in every direction. In the same way, a person who sees everything as separate keeps running after many different things.

upanishads-katha-2-1-15.plain: Pure water poured into pure water becomes one and stays pure. Death tells Nachiketas, whom he calls Gautama after his family, that the Self of a wise knower becomes one with the highest reality in the same way.

upanishads-katha-2-2-1.plain: The body is like a town with eleven gates, the body's openings, where Brahman, the Unborn, lives. Brahman's thinking is never crooked. Whoever turns to it stops grieving and becomes truly free.
themes: body as a home for the soul

upanishads-chandogya-7-2-1.plain: The teacher Sanatkumara tells his student Narada that speech is greater than names. Without speech we could not know the sacred books, the world around us, or the difference between right and wrong, true and false, good and bad.

upanishads-chandogya-7-2-2.plain: Whoever honors speech as Brahman (the highest reality) has mastery as far as speech can reach. Narada asks if there is something greater than speech, and the teacher says yes.

upanishads-chandogya-7-3-1.plain: The mind is greater than speech, because it holds both speech and names, the way a closed fist holds a couple of small fruits. Whatever a person decides in their mind to read, do or wish for, they then do it.

upanishads-chandogya-7-3-2.plain: Whoever honors the mind as Brahman has mastery as far as the mind reaches. Narada asks for something greater than the mind, and the teacher agrees to tell him.

upanishads-chandogya-7-4-1.plain: Will, meaning firm intention or resolve, is greater than the mind. First a person resolves, then thinks, then speaks, and the words come out as names, which hold the sacred hymns and rituals.

upanishads-chandogya-7-4-2.plain: Everything from thinking to ritual rests on will. The teacher describes the whole world as a chain of intention: sky and earth lead to rain, rain to food, food to life, and so on until everything has its purpose.

upanishads-chandogya-7-4-3.plain: Whoever honors will as Brahman becomes safe, steady and free of distress, and reaches the steady worlds they have intended. Narada asks for something greater than will.

upanishads-chandogya-7-5-1.plain: Consideration, meaning careful thoughtful attention, is greater than will. A person first considers, then resolves, then thinks, then speaks.

upanishads-chandogya-7-5-2.plain: A thoughtless person is ignored even if they know a lot, while a thoughtful person who knows little is gladly listened to. Thoughtfulness is the center and support of everything else.

upanishads-chandogya-7-5-3.plain: Whoever honors consideration as Brahman becomes safe, steady and free of distress and has mastery as far as it reaches. Narada asks for something still greater.

upanishads-chandogya-7-6-1.plain: Reflection, meaning quiet deep meditation, is greater than consideration. The earth, sky and mountains seem still as if meditating, and great people show the same calm, while small-minded people are always quarreling, insulting and gossiping.

upanishads-chandogya-7-6-2.plain: Whoever honors reflection as Brahman has mastery as far as reflection reaches. Narada asks for something greater than reflection.

upanishads-chandogya-7-7-1.plain: Understanding is greater than reflection. Through understanding we grasp the sacred books, the whole natural world, right and wrong, true and false, and this world and the next.

upanishads-chandogya-7-7-2.plain: Whoever honors understanding as Brahman reaches worlds full of knowledge and has mastery as far as understanding reaches. Narada asks for something greater.

upanishads-chandogya-7-8-1.plain: Strength is greater than understanding, since one strong person can shake a hundred clever ones. With strength a person gets up, seeks out wise people, follows them, and comes to truly see and understand; strength also holds the whole world steady.

upanishads-chandogya-7-8-2.plain: Whoever honors strength as Brahman has mastery as far as strength reaches. Narada asks for something greater than strength.

upanishads-chandogya-7-9-1.plain: Food is greater than strength. If a person goes without food for ten days, they may live but cannot see, hear, think or act properly; once they eat, these powers return.

upanishads-chandogya-7-9-2.plain: Whoever honors food as Brahman gains worlds rich in food and drink and has mastery as far as food reaches. Narada asks for something greater than food.

upanishads-chandogya-7-10-1.plain: Water is greater than food. When rain fails, living beings grow afraid there will be little food, and when rain is plentiful they rejoice; water takes the shape of the earth, sky, mountains and all living things.

upanishads-chandogya-7-10-2.plain: Whoever honors water as Brahman gets all their wishes and feels satisfied, with mastery as far as water reaches. Narada asks for something greater than water.

upanishads-chandogya-3-19-2.plain: The story of the cosmic egg continues. The silver half of the egg became the earth and the golden half became the sky. The egg's inner skins became the mountains and the clouds, its little veins became the rivers, and its liquid became the sea.
themes: wonder at the earth and sky

upanishads-chandogya-3-19-3.plain: The sun was born from the egg. When it was born, everyone shouted with joy, and all living beings and all the things they wished for came into being. That is why people still cheer and come alive whenever the sun rises and sets.

upanishads-chandogya-3-19-4.plain: A person who knows this story and meditates on the sun as Brahman, the highest reality, will be surrounded by happy, joyful sounds, and that joy will stay with them.

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-1.plain: Long ago there lived a king named Janashruti, the great-grandson of Janashruta. He was very generous. He gave away lots of wealth, kept his home open to guests, and built shelters everywhere so people could eat his food.

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-2.plain: One night some swan-like birds flew over the king's house. One bird called to another, "Hey, short-sighted friend! The king's glory has spread like the sky. Don't fly too close or it will burn you."

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-3.plain: The second bird answered, "Why do you talk about this noble king as if he were as great as Raikva, the man with the cart?"

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-4.plain: The first bird asked who this Raikva was. The second bird explained that just as the winning throw in a dice game takes all the lower throws, all the good that other people do is included in Raikva. That is because Raikva knows the highest truth.

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-5.plain: The king overheard the birds. In the morning he asked his servant whether people spoke of him as if he were like Raikva with the cart. The servant asked who Raikva was.

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-6.plain: The king repeated what the bird had said: just as the winning dice throw takes all the others, all the good that others do belongs to Raikva, because he knows the highest truth.

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-7.plain: The servant went to find Raikva but came back saying he could not find him. The king told him to look in the quiet, lonely places where a holy man would live.

upanishads-chandogya-4-1-8.plain: The servant found a man lying under a cart and scratching his sores. He asked, "Sir, are you Raikva with the cart?" The man said, "Here I am." The servant went back and told the king he had found him.

upanishads-chandogya-4-2-1.plain: The king took six hundred cows, a necklace, and a cart pulled by mules, and went to see Raikva.

upanishads-chandogya-4-2-2.plain: The king said, "Raikva, here are six hundred cows, a necklace, and a mule cart. Please teach me about the god you worship."

upanishads-chandogya-4-2-3.plain: Raikva refused rudely. He called the king a Shudra, a man of low rank, and told him to keep his gifts. So the king came back with a thousand cows, a necklace, a mule cart, and his own daughter.

upanishads-chandogya-4-2-4.plain: The king said, "Raikva, here are a thousand cows, a necklace, a mule cart, this wife, and the village where you live. Sir, please teach me!"

upanishads-chandogya-4-2-5.plain: Raikva lifted the young woman's face and said that the king's gifts alone had not moved him; it was this that made him agree to speak. The villages he lived in, in the land of the Mahavrishas, became known as Raikva-parna. Then he began to teach the king.

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-1.plain: Raikva teaches that air is where everything ends up. When fire goes out, when the sun sets, and when the moon sets, they all go into the air.
themes: where things go when they end

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-2.plain: When water dries up, it also goes into air. Air takes in all of these things. This is the teaching about the forces of nature, the Devas or gods.
themes: where things go when they end

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-3.plain: In the same way, inside the body, breath (prana, the life-breath) is where everything ends up. When a person sleeps, speech, sight, hearing, and the mind all go back into the breath. Breath takes them all in.

upanishads-chandogya-4-3-4.plain: Raikva sums up: there are two things everything goes into. Outside, among the forces of nature, it is air. Inside, among the senses, it is breath.

upanishads-kena-3-9.plain: The mysterious being, which is Brahman (the one supreme reality behind everything), asks Vayu, the god of wind, what power he has. Vayu boasts that he could lift and carry off everything on earth.

upanishads-kena-3-10.plain: Brahman puts a single straw in front of Vayu and tells him to lift it. Vayu tries with all his strength but cannot move it, so he goes back and admits he could not find out who this being is.

upanishads-kena-3-11.plain: Next the gods ask Indra, their king (also called Maghavan, 'the generous one'), to find out who the being is. But when Indra comes near, the being disappears.
themes: the divine is hard to grasp

upanishads-kena-3-12.plain: In that same space Indra meets a beautifully dressed woman, Uma, daughter of Himavat, the Himalaya mountain. He asks her who that being was.

upanishads-kena-4-1.plain: Uma tells Indra that the being was Brahman. She explains that the gods won their victory only because of Brahman's power, not their own. Then Indra understood it was Brahman.
themes: success is not only my doing

upanishads-kena-4-2.plain: Because Agni (fire), Vayu (wind) and Indra came closest to Brahman, they are honored above the other gods.

upanishads-kena-4-3.plain: Indra is honored most of all, because he came nearest to Brahman and was the first to know it.

upanishads-kena-4-4.plain: In nature, Brahman can be pictured like a flash of lightning: it shines out for a moment and then is gone again.
themes: God is hard to hold onto

upanishads-kena-4-5.plain: Inside us, Brahman is what seems to move as the mind. It is what lets us imagine and remember things again and again.

upanishads-kena-4-6.plain: Brahman is called Tadvana, meaning 'the one everyone longs for,' and one should meditate on it by that name. A person who knows this is loved by all beings.

upanishads-kena-4-7.plain: The teacher tells the student that he has now given the secret teaching that was asked for. This is the teaching about Brahman.

upanishads-kena-4-8.plain: The teacher says this teaching rests on self-discipline, self-control and selfless giving. The holy books, the Vedas, support it, and truth is its home.
themes: how to prepare for spiritual growth

upanishads-kena-4-9.plain: Whoever truly understands this teaching and leaves all wrongdoing behind reaches a heaven that is endless and can never be lost.

upanishads-katha-1-1-1.plain: A man named Vajasravasa, hoping for rewards in heaven, held a ritual where he promised to give away everything he owned. He had a son named Nachiketas.

upanishads-katha-1-1-2.plain: While the gifts were being handed to the priests, the boy Nachiketas was filled with deep faith and began to think hard about what he saw.

upanishads-katha-1-1-3.plain: Nachiketas thinks that giving away old, worn-out cows that can no longer eat, drink or give milk brings no blessing. Such a gift is empty and does no good.

upanishads-katha-1-1-4.plain: Since his father had promised to give away everything, Nachiketas asks him three times, 'To whom will you give me?' His father angrily answers, 'I give you to Death.'

upanishads-katha-1-1-5.plain: Nachiketas reflects that he is neither the first nor the last to die. He wonders what Yama, the god of death, will do with him.

upanishads-katha-1-1-6.plain: Nachiketas says to look at those who lived before and those who will come after. People grow old and die like grain, and like grain they are born again.

upanishads-katha-1-1-7.plain: Nachiketas arrives at Death's house and waits there. Voices remind Yama (here called Vaivasvata, son of the Sun) that a holy guest is like a fire in the home and must be welcomed with water and kindness.

upanishads-chandogya-5-12-1.plain: King Asvapati asks the scholar Aupamanyava what he worships as the Self, the deepest reality. He says heaven. The king answers that heaven is one part of Vaisvanara, the universal Self present in all things, called 'the one with good light,' and that this is why his house is full of rituals.

upanishads-chandogya-5-12-2.plain: The king says that worshipping heaven brings food, the things one wishes for, and religious honor to one's home. But heaven is only the head of the universal Self. Seeing only one part could have led Aupamanyava to disaster, and coming to learn more saved him.
themes: seeing only part of the truth

upanishads-chandogya-5-13-1.plain: The king asks Satyayajna what he worships as the Self, and he says the sun. The king says the sun is one part of the universal Self, called 'many-formed,' and that is why his house has many kinds of wealth.

upanishads-chandogya-5-13-2.plain: The king says the sun-worshipper has carriages, servants and jewels, food and the things he wishes for. But the sun is only the eye of the universal Self. Without the fuller teaching he might have gone blind.
themes: seeing only part of the truth

upanishads-chandogya-5-14-1.plain: The king asks Indradyumna what he worships as the Self, and he says the air. The king says air is one part of the universal Self, the one that 'moves in many paths.' That is why gifts reach him from many directions and many carriages follow him.

upanishads-chandogya-5-14-2.plain: The king says the air-worshipper is blessed with food, wishes and honor. But air is only the breath of the universal Self. Without the fuller teaching his breath might have left him.
themes: seeing only part of the truth

upanishads-chandogya-5-15-1.plain: The king asks Jana what he worships as the Self, and he says space, the open sky that holds everything. The king says space is one part of the universal Self, called 'the full one.' That is why Jana has many children and much wealth.

upanishads-chandogya-5-15-2.plain: The king says space-worship brings food, wishes and honor. But space is only the body, or trunk, of the universal Self. Without the fuller teaching Jana's body might have perished.
themes: seeing only part of the truth

upanishads-chandogya-5-16-1.plain: The king asks Budila what he worships as the Self, and he says water. The king says water is one part of the universal Self, called 'wealth.' That is why Budila is rich and thriving.

upanishads-chandogya-5-16-2.plain: The king says water-worship brings food, wishes and honor. But water is only the bladder of the universal Self. Without the fuller teaching Budila's bladder might have burst.
themes: seeing only part of the truth

upanishads-chandogya-5-17-1.plain: The king asks Uddalaka Aruni what he worships as the Self, and he says the earth. The king says earth is one part of the universal Self, called 'firm support.' That is why Uddalaka stands secure with children and cattle.

upanishads-chandogya-5-17-2.plain: The king says earth-worship brings food, wishes and honor. But the earth is only the feet of the universal Self. Without the fuller teaching Uddalaka's feet might have given way.
themes: seeing only part of the truth

upanishads-chandogya-5-18-1.plain: The king tells all six scholars that each of them saw the universal Self in pieces, as if it were many things. Whoever knows it as one whole, living inside himself and the same as his own self, is nourished in all worlds and in all beings.

upanishads-chandogya-5-18-2.plain: The king describes the universal Self as one body. Heaven is its head, the sun its eye, air its breath, space its trunk, water its bladder, and earth its feet. Its chest, hair, heart, mind and mouth are the altar, the altar grass, and the three sacred fires.

upanishads-chandogya-5-19-1.plain: The king teaches that eating is itself a sacred offering. The first bite of a meal should be offered to Prana, the breath that moves upward, while saying 'Svaha,' the word spoken when making an offering. This satisfies that breath.

upanishads-chandogya-5-19-2.plain: When this breath is satisfied, the eye, the sun, heaven and everything beneath them are satisfied too. Through this, the person eating is blessed with children, cattle, health, radiance and spiritual glory.

upanishads-chandogya-5-20-1.plain: The second bite of food should be offered to Vyana, the breath that spreads through the whole body, while saying 'Svaha.' This satisfies that breath.

upanishads-chandogya-5-20-2.plain: When this breath is satisfied, the ear, the moon, the directions of space and everything beneath them are satisfied. Through this, the person eating is blessed with children, cattle, health, radiance and spiritual glory.

upanishads-chandogya-5-21-1.plain: The third bite should be offered to Apana, the breath that moves downward, while saying 'Svaha.' This satisfies the tongue, fire, the earth and everything beneath them.

upanishads-chandogya-5-21-2.plain: Through all of them being satisfied, the person eating is blessed with children, cattle, health, radiance and spiritual glory.

upanishads-chandogya-3-9-3.plain: A person who understands this fourth nectar joins the Maruts, the storm gods led by Soma, the moon god. Like them, he enjoys the nectar just by looking at it, and he rests in its color and rises from it again.

upanishads-chandogya-3-9-4.plain: This verse describes a huge stretch of cosmic time, told as the sun rising and setting from different directions. For that whole age, the knower shares the rule of the Maruts, the storm gods.

upanishads-chandogya-3-10-1.plain: The fifth nectar of the sun belongs to the Sadhyas, a group of heavenly beings led by Brahman, here meaning the creator. The gods do not eat or drink it; they are filled with joy just by seeing it.

upanishads-chandogya-3-10-2.plain: The Sadhyas rest within the color of this nectar and come out from it again, as if resting and then rising to enjoy it.

upanishads-chandogya-3-10-3.plain: A person who understands this fifth nectar becomes one of the Sadhyas, led by Brahman the creator. He sees the nectar and is happy, and he rests in its color and rises from it again.

upanishads-chandogya-3-10-4.plain: This describes an even longer age of the universe, told as the sun rising and setting in new directions. For that whole time, the knower shares the power of the Sadhyas.

upanishads-chandogya-3-11-1.plain: After all these ages, the sun rises up and no longer rises or sets at all. It stays alone in the center, and a verse is quoted about this.

upanishads-chandogya-3-11-2.plain: The verse says that there, the sun never rises and never sets. The speaker swears by the gods that this is true, and says he would lose Brahman, the ultimate reality, if it were not.

upanishads-chandogya-3-11-3.plain: For the person who truly knows this secret teaching about Brahman, the ultimate reality, the sun no longer rises or sets. For him it is day forever.

upanishads-chandogya-3-11-4.plain: This teaching was handed down from the creator god to Prajapati, then to Manu the first man, then to his descendants. Finally, a father passed it on to the sage Uddalaka Aruni.

upanishads-chandogya-3-11-5.plain: So a father should teach this knowledge of Brahman only to his eldest son or a worthy student. He should not give it to anyone else, even for the whole treasure-filled earth, because it is worth more than all of that.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-1.plain: The Gayatri, a famous sacred verse, is said to be everything that exists. It is also speech, because speech sings out and protects all things.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-2.plain: The Gayatri is also the earth, because everything that exists rests on the earth and does not go beyond it.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-3.plain: The earth is like the human body, because the body holds the life-breaths, called pranas, which keep us alive.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-4.plain: The body in turn is like the heart inside a person, because the life-breaths rest in the heart and do not go beyond it.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-5.plain: The Gayatri verse has four parts, or feet, and six aspects. A verse from the Rig Veda, the oldest scripture, is quoted to support this.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-6.plain: The quoted verse says the Person, the Supreme Being, is even greater than all this. All created things are only one quarter of him, and the other three quarters are immortal, beyond this world.
themes: God is greater than the world

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-7.plain: This Brahman, the ultimate reality just described, is the same as the open space all around us.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-8.plain: The space around us is the same as the space inside us. Outside and inside are one.

upanishads-chandogya-3-12-9.plain: The space inside us is the space within the heart. That space is Brahman, present everywhere and never changing. Whoever knows this gains a happiness that is everywhere and never changes.
